articles.title: Cinderella panto set to enchant audiences at Middleton Arena this Christmas
articles.excerpt: Panto-goers in Middleton will soon be treated to a magical rendition of Cinderella at Middleton Arena, starting December 20. The production features Becca Elizabeth-Davies as Cinderella and Tom Sentia as Prince Charming, who embarks on a quest to find the owner of a special glass slipper.
articles.content_html:
Panto-goers in Middleton will soon be treated to a magical rendition of Cinderella at Middleton Arena, starting December 20.

The production features Becca Elizabeth-Davies as Cinderella and Tom Sentia as Prince Charming, who embarks on a quest to find the owner of a special glass slipper.

Joining them is Amy Dowden from Strictly Come Dancing, who will play The Fairy Godmother, guiding Cinderella as she dreams of escaping her life with her wicked stepsisters, portrayed by Craig Colley and Jon Hands.

Alex Bain, known for his role in Coronation Street, will take on the character of Dandini, while Chris Johnson returns as Buttons, a role he has previously performed.

Middleton Arena has described the show as the biggest ball of the season, inviting families to join Cinderella and her friends in this enchanting fairy tale.

The production promises to be a festive highlight for the community, bringing together audiences of all ages to celebrate the spirit of Christmas.

As the opening date approaches, local families are encouraged to secure their tickets early to avoid disappointment. This annual panto is a cherished tradition, offering a delightful experience filled with laughter and joy during the festive season.

articles.title: Did goblins move Rochdale Parish Church up the hill?
articles.excerpt: A long-told local tale says unseen workers carried building stones overnight to the top of the hill; the record shows a medieval church, later Victorian work, and a 19th‑century storyteller rather than supernatural masons.
articles.summary: A long-told local tale says unseen workers carried building stones overnight to the top of the hill; the record shows a medieval church, later Victorian work, and a 19th‑century storyteller rather than supernatural masons.
articles.body:
The short answer is: no, there is no evidence that goblins or other supernatural creatures physically moved the stones of St Chad’s Church. That story belongs to Lancashire folklore, best known from the 19th‑century collector John Roby, while the documentary and architectural record shows a long‑standing church site with medieval fabric and later restorations. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

Roby’s version of the tale — titled “The Goblin Builders” in his Traditions of Lancashire — describes a Saxon thane, piles of building stone laid by the river, and those materials mysteriously transferred overnight to the hill where St Chad’s now stands; Roby also notes the famous flight of steps (he records 124) leading up to the church. That account is a clear piece of local storytelling rather than a contemporary record of building work. Roby wrote in the 19th century as a folklorist and compiler of oral tradition; his retelling preserves how people in his era understood the place, not the legal or archaeological history of its masoning. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

The documented history of the building is plain and far less sensational. Historic England lists St Chad’s as Grade II* and describes medieval and post‑medieval construction phases: a thirteenth‑century tower, fourteenth‑century arcade columns and arches, a clerestory dated 1557, and substantial Victorian restorations and additions in the 19th century. Those layers — Norman and medieval masonry altered, repaired and refashioned over centuries — explain the church’s position and appearance more plausibly than an overnight relocation by invisible hands. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

Why on the hill? Practical and symbolic reasons usually guided medieval siting. A high position overlooks the river and the town, keeps the building clear of floodplain, and gives the church civic and visual prominence; these are the kinds of factors architectural historians use when they discuss hilltop parish churches, and they match the description of St Chad’s occupying high ground above the River Roch. The building’s long use as the mother church of the ancient parish of Rochdale — serving a large rural parish for many centuries — also favoured a prominent site. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

That is not to say the legend has no local value. Roby’s telling and other versions preserve a communal memory that the church’s siting felt important enough to explain with a story; the goblin motif is widespread in English folklore as a way to name unexplained or surprising events. Local guides and walking routes still point out the steps and repeat the tale; it’s part of how Rochdale people have talked about their church across generations. But folklore and documentary history are different tools: the former explains meaning, the latter records evidence. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

If you want to check the facts in person: the parish continues to use St Chad’s as Rochdale Parish Church, and the building, its steps and the churchyard are publicly accessible; the parish’s information pages list services and contact details. For the architectural inventory, Historic England’s official list entry gives the formal description and dating used by planners and conservators. If any reader is curious about the Roby story itself, his Traditions of Lancashire is available in full online as a 19th‑century account of local legend. ([rochdalecommunity.org.uk](https://rochdalecommunity.org.uk/sites/saint-chad-rochdale-parish-church/))

articles.title: Rochdale Leisure Centre small pool closed for repairs
articles.excerpt: The small pool at Rochdale Leisure Centre is closed until further notice due to a technical issue with its movable floor, affecting scheduled sessions.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Leisure Centre has announced the closure of its small pool due to ongoing technical issues with the movable floor. The facility is currently awaiting assistance from a specialist external contractor to resolve the problem.

As a result of this closure, all scheduled sessions for the small pool on Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays have been cancelled until further notice. The management has expressed apologies for any inconvenience this may cause to users.

This closure affects local residents who rely on the small pool for swimming lessons, recreational swimming, and other aquatic activities. The leisure centre is a key facility for health and fitness in the Rochdale area, making this closure significant for the community.

The management is working to restore normal service as quickly as possible and appreciates the patience and understanding of its users during this time.

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.summary: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.body:
Short answer: the house at Clegg Hall is real; the boggart belongs to folklore.

Clegg Hall stands on Clegg Hall Road, near Smithy Bridge (Milnrow) about two miles north‑east of Rochdale. The building you can see today is a protected, Grade II* listed house whose main fabric dates to about 1610; Historic England records that listing (List Entry 1309615, first listed 10 August 1951) and gives the architectural description and location. Those are verifiable, recent and public facts. The “boggart” stories are an older, oral and literary tradition layered over that solid record. 

What the documents say: local and county histories trace the place-name and family back to the medieval era but do not confirm the grisly crime the legend describes. Victorian county compilers and parish historians — the sources relied on by Historic England — record that the medieval Clegg family held land here, but that their holding had changed hands by the late 1200s and that later documentary evidence for a family murder is absent. In short: there is no surviving contemporary legal or parish record that corroborates the tale of an uncle murdering heirs by throwing them into a moat. (These points are set out in the local histories cited in the Historic England listing and in the History of the Parish of Rochdale.)

What the storytellers say: the best‑known version of the boggart appears in 19th‑century folklore collections. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and other collectors printed lively accounts of a “Clegg‑Hall Boggart” — a malign household spirit variously called “Noman” in retellings — and filled them with theatrical incidents: a boggart chamber, a conjuring scene that includes the mock‑baptism of a fowl, and a supposed murderous plot to seize an inheritance. These tellings are valuable as folklore — they show how local people and writers shaped place and memory — but they are literary and oral sources written long after the events they describe. They do not stand in for primary legal evidence.

How historians and archivists treat the story: county historians and the Victoria County History tradition treat the Roby‑style tales as imaginative reconstructions rather than archival reportage. That judgement matters: antiquarian and folkloric writers of the 18th and 19th centuries enthusiastically collected local stories, but they also embroidered and adapted them for drama and moral lesson. Where a claim concerns a violent death or other serious matter, historians look for surviving deeds, court rolls, wills or parish registers. For Clegg Hall, those contemporary anchors for the boggart narrative are missing in the published local record.

Does anybody claim to have recent proof of a haunting? No. There is no official inspection, police finding, archaeological report or archival discovery published in primary sources that confirms the supernatural elements of the Clegg Hall tales. The house remains private property and its architectural listing is the public record that governs what the council and the public can rely on. If anyone hopes for an authoritative update (for example a newly found medieval deed or a published archaeological survey), that would need to appear in named archival catalogues, a local authority report or a recognised academic publication before it could alter the basic separation between folklore and documented history.

What readers can do and where to look next: if you want the verifiable facts about the building and its legal status, start with Historic England’s National Heritage List entry (List Entry 1309615). For the folklore side, read the contemporary printed collections such as John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and the 19th‑century county histories (often available in digitised form). If you want archival confirmation one way or another, Rochdale local studies and archives and the county record offices hold the primary material historians would consult; ask them for searches of deeds, manorial records and parish registers for Clegg/Clegg Hall — but be clear: until such primary documents are published or cited, the boggart remains a durable piece of local storytelling rather than a documented historical fact.

Verdict for the reader: Clegg Hall’s building and location are verifiable; its boggart lives in the region’s printed and oral folklore. That’s not the same as proof of a haunting or of a medieval murder supported by contemporary records. For now, the boggart is a good story worth retelling — and a reminder to treat nineteenth‑century folklore as a literary and cultural source, not a court roll.

articles.title: Middleton care worker celebrated after 27 years at Langfield Care Home
articles.excerpt: Karen Haycock, who joined Langfield Care Home in Langley in May 1999, was surprised by colleagues and residents marking what the home calls 10,000 days of service.
articles.content_html:
A support worker at a Middleton care home has been celebrated by colleagues and residents after more than 27 years of looking after people at the home.

Karen Haycock, a specialist support worker at Langfield Care Home on Wood Street, Langley, was surprised with gifts, flowers and cards at a gathering on 27 October.

The home is marking the occasion as 10,000 days of service. Karen joined the home’s operator, Orchard Healthcare Group, in May 1999 — roughly 10,000 days ago — so the milestone reflects the length of her time with the home rather than a count of individual shifts.

Over her career Karen has worked across residential care, dementia care and nursing. She now works in the home’s Reconnect dementia community, which supports residents living with advanced dementia.

Along the way she completed an NVQ Level 2, took part in Orchard’s Step Up programme and undertook specialist Dementia Promise training. The group says she has seen the sector change considerably in that time, with better specialist training, equipment and more individual approaches to caring for people with dementia.

For Karen, though, the job is still about people. “I love spending time with the residents. They become your family,” she said.

Asked what she would tell anyone thinking about a career in care, she said: “You need to give it 100% to be able to make a difference to people, and that’s the best part.”

Home manager Lisa-Marie Hutchinson said: “Karen’s 10,000 working days is a fantastic achievement, and we were delighted to celebrate this special milestone with her and show her how much she is appreciated.”

Long service of this kind is increasingly rare in adult social care, where staff turnover is high and many homes rely on a changing workforce. For residents living with dementia, a familiar face who has known the home for decades can make a real difference to day-to-day life and to families choosing care for a relative.

Langfield is one of 23 care homes run by Harrogate-based Orchard Healthcare Group across the North of England and the Midlands. The group says the home holds a Good rating from the Care Quality Commission.

articles.title: Missed the secondary school deadline in Rochdale? What parents need to do next
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's 31 October deadline has passed, but families can still apply for a Year 7 place for September 2027. Here is how late applications are handled and when offers are expected.
articles.content_html:
Families who missed Rochdale borough's secondary school application deadline can still submit an application for a Year 7 place starting in September 2027. The council's closing date was Saturday, 31 October 2026, but its online Parent Portal remains the route for late applications.

The important difference is when the application will be considered. Rochdale Borough Council says applications received after the deadline are not processed until after national offer day on Monday, 1 March 2027, because applications submitted on time take priority. Schools do not reserve places for late applicants, so a preferred school may already be full when a late application is assessed.

Parents are advised to list all five school preferences, rather than naming only one school. The council uses its normal published admissions criteria to allocate places remaining after the on-time round. Naming a single preference does not increase the chance of securing that school.

For late applications made before 1 March 2027, the council aims to issue an offer by Friday, 30 April 2027. Applications made from 1 March to 19 March are expected to receive an offer by Friday, 7 May. Applications submitted after 19 March are handled on a later timetable set out in the council's admissions guidance. These are target dates, not guarantees of a particular school.

Children who live in Rochdale borough must apply through Rochdale Borough Council even if a preferred school is outside the borough. Families living in another local authority area should apply through their home council, including any Rochdale schools among their preferences. Some faith schools and academies may require supplementary evidence, which must be supplied to the school itself.

Parents should keep the email confirming submission. The council advises applicants to resubmit their form after making changes in the Parent Portal. Families needing help can contact the school admissions team at school.admissions@rochdale.gov.uk or 0300 303 0340, Monday to Friday, 9am to 4.45pm.

The council's current application instructions, late-offer timetable and Parent Portal link are at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/school-admissions-appeals/apply-secondary-school-place/4.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards contract for family temporary accommodation services
articles.excerpt: The Bond Board Limited has been awarded a contract to manage the Homeless Family Leasing Scheme, providing vital support to homeless families in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract for the management and support services of the Homeless Family Leasing Scheme (HFLS) to The Bond Board Limited. This initiative aims to provide essential tenancy management and support for homeless families placed in temporary accommodation.

The HFLS will oversee approximately 40 leased properties, offering services that include property management, tenancy sustainment, and move-on support. This contract is part of the council's ongoing efforts to address homelessness in the area and provide stable housing solutions for families in need.

In addition to the HFLS contract, the council has also awarded a separate contract for the A Bed for Every Night (ABEN) Dispersed Accommodation and Support Services to Stepping Stone Projects.

This service will provide around 34 units of accommodation for homeless individuals and those at risk of rough sleeping, along with housing-related support to help them achieve stable living conditions.

These contracts are significant steps in tackling homelessness in Rochdale, reflecting the council's commitment to supporting vulnerable families and individuals. The Bond Board Limited and Stepping Stone Projects are expected to begin their services shortly, contributing to the local community's efforts to reduce homelessness.

articles.title: Mark Winstanley returns to stage after MS diagnosis for Rochdale comedy show
articles.excerpt: Actor Mark Winstanley will perform in 'Cabaret Schmabaret' at the Ukrainian Centre on 19 November, marking his return to the stage after a five-year hiatus due to multiple sclerosis.
articles.content_html:
Actor Mark Winstanley is set to return to the stage after a five-year break following his diagnosis with multiple sclerosis. He will perform in 'Cabaret Schmabaret' at the Ukrainian Centre in Rochdale on 19 November, bringing his comedic talents back to the local audience.

Winstanley, who co-runs the Manchester-based theatre company The Performers’ Playground with Alice Robinson, has a rich history in theatre, having performed nationally and internationally with various touring companies.

His return is particularly significant as it showcases his resilience and commitment to the arts despite his health challenges.

In addition to 'Cabaret Schmabaret', The Performers’ Playground is also fundraising for a separate production of 'Ubu Royale', which is currently in research and development. This production is designed to accommodate Winstanley's mobility and fatigue issues, with plans for a national tour in 2027.

Winstanley's comeback not only highlights his personal journey but also serves as an inspiration for others facing similar challenges. Local audiences can look forward to enjoying a unique comedic experience while supporting a talented artist's return to the stage.

articles.title: Birthday cards for Wendy: family’s heartfelt appeal ahead of her 79th birthday
articles.excerpt: Wendy Bamford turns 79 on Wednesday 4 November, and her birthday wish is simple: cards filled with kind words.
articles.content_html:
A family is inviting the community to help make Wendy Bamford’s 79th birthday special by sending her a card filled with a few kind words.

Wendy turns 79 on Wednesday 4 November. Her son Stephen Bamford shared the appeal after she moved to Springhill Hospice in Rochdale.

When he asked his mum what she wanted for her birthday, or whether there was anything she would like to do, her answer was simple: lots of birthday cards, so she could sit and read the lovely messages inside. It is the only thing she has asked for, Stephen said.

A little kindness could mean so much

Stephen is welcoming cards from people who know Wendy and those who have never met her but would like to brighten her day.

“A few kind words might seem like a small thing, but they would mean the world to her right now,” he wrote.

In an update, Stephen thanked everyone for their comments and messages, explaining that the response had become too large for him to answer individually. He shared two addresses where cards can be sent.

Where to send a birthday card

Cards can be addressed directly to Wendy at:

Wendy Bamford, Room 10, Springhill Hospice, Broad Lane, Rochdale

Alternatively, cards can be sent to Stephen through the Littleborough collection address:

For Wendy Bamford, care of Stephen Bamford, Cryers Butchers, 39 Victoria Street, Littleborough, OL15 8BA

Stephen has promised to make sure his mum receives them, ready to open and enjoy on her birthday. Anyone wishing to take part is encouraged to allow time for delivery.

articles.title: Heywood’s Little Play Town put up for sale as owner reassures families it will stay open
articles.excerpt: Owner Jackie is seeking a buyer after four years, with Little Play Town remaining open and existing party bookings going ahead as planned.
articles.content_html:
Little Play Town in Heywood has been put up for sale, with owner Jackie reassuring families that the children’s role play business will remain open and existing party bookings will go ahead as planned.

Announcing the decision, Jackie said she was selling for personal reasons after four years of building the business alongside her team.

“This is something I never thought I’d be writing, and it’s been an incredibly difficult decision to make,” she said.

Jackie described Little Play Town as her “pride and joy” and thanked the staff, customers and families who have supported it.

She stressed that the sale announcement does not mean the venue is closing. Sessions will continue as normal, and families with parties booked do not need to change their plans.

The search is now on for a new owner to take over the established leasehold business. Jackie said a support package lasting up to three months would be available to help the buyer settle in.

The announcement highlights the existing staff team, supportive customer base and opportunities to introduce additional themed events, sessions and experiences. Jackie also described the landlord as proactive and supportive.

She hopes to find someone who will build on the business’s first four years and continue providing a place for children to play and make memories.

Anyone interested in buying Little Play Town can register their interest by emailing info@littleplaytownheywood.co.uk.

articles.title: Eight winners honoured at Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Diversity Awards celebrated eight winners for their contributions to equality and community cohesion at a ceremony attended by over 350 guests.
articles.content_html:
More than 350 guests gathered at Rochdale Town Hall on October 30, 2026, for the Rochdale Diversity Awards, which recognised eight winners for their outstanding contributions to equality, diversity, and community cohesion across the borough.

Organised by the Kashmir Youth Project (KYP), the awards celebrated the achievements of individuals and organisations that have made significant impacts in promoting inclusivity. This year, the event received over 130 nominations, showcasing the breadth of community engagement in Rochdale.

Among the winners, Rochdale Science Initiative C.I.C. received the Breaking Barriers Award, while its founder, Mohammed Attaur Rahman, was honoured with the Outstanding Achievement in Diversity Award.

Other notable recognitions included the Diversity in Public Sector Partnership Working Award, awarded to Petrus and the Rochdale Community Safety Team for their Town Centre Outreach Initiative.

The awards, which KYP has delivered since 2012, highlight the importance of fostering a diverse and inclusive community. The recognition of these efforts not only celebrates individual achievements but also encourages ongoing commitment to equality and cohesion in Rochdale.

Following the Middleton event, a second fireworks display will take place on November 3 at Queen’s Park Road in Heywood, also beginning at 7:30pm. This event is expected to attract local families and residents looking to enjoy the Bonfire Night festivities.

The final event in the series will occur on November 4 at Cronkeyshaw Common, rounding off the celebrations with another fireworks display at the same time. Each event aims to provide a safe and enjoyable experience for attendees of all ages.

These celebrations are significant for the local community, offering a chance for families to come together and enjoy the traditional Bonfire Night festivities. Residents are encouraged to attend and participate in the celebrations.

articles.title: Scrooge screening with live orchestra comes to Heywood Civic
articles.excerpt: The 1951 film starring Alastair Sim will be shown with a live score from the three-piece FB Pocket Orchestra on Saturday 14 November.
articles.content_html:
A screening of the classic film Scrooge with a live three-piece orchestra is coming to Heywood Civic on Saturday 14 November.

The event starts at 8pm and pairs the 1951 film starring Alastair Sim with music performed by the FB Pocket Orchestra. The production is touring in the film’s 75th anniversary year.

The venue lists a running time of 90 minutes. Its Pay What You Can prices are £8.40 at the lower rate, £10.50 standard and £12.60 at the higher rate, all including the booking fee.

Rather than a stage adaptation, this is a showing of the film with live musical accompaniment. It follows Ebenezer Scrooge’s encounters with the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Future in the familiar Charles Dickens story.

The organisers say the music is based on Richard Addinsell’s original score. Heywood Civic’s listing explains that Paul Stevenson reconstructed the score by listening to and transcribing the film soundtrack, creating an arrangement for the ensemble.

The film has a U certificate. For local families and cinema fans, the event offers a chance to hear live musicians accompany a black-and-white Christmas classic at a borough venue.

Heywood Civic is on LCpl Stephen Shaw MC Way, Heywood, OL10 1LW. Tickets and the venue’s pricing information are available at https://heywoodcivic.co.uk/event/scrooge-u-live-to-film/. Check availability and the venue’s accessibility information before booking.

The event was announced in a press release supplied by FB Music and Media, with the date, running time and ticket prices checked against Heywood Civic’s listing on 28 October 2026.

articles.title: Rochdale Council awards contract for Queen's Park SEND improvement project
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to enhance the play area at Queen's Park, Heywood, focusing on inclusivity for children with special educational needs.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract to MASSEY & HARRIS (ENGINEERING) LIMITED for the Queen's Park SEND and Improvement Project. This initiative aims to create a more inclusive play area at Queen's Park in Heywood, enhancing facilities for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The project will involve several key improvements, including the extension of the existing play area, the installation of a dance arch, the creation of a sensory area surrounding the dance arch, and the addition of a wheelchair swing.

These enhancements are designed to ensure that all children can enjoy the park's facilities, regardless of their physical abilities.

articles.title: The priest, the chicken and the shoe: Rochdale’s strangest boggart story
articles.excerpt: A gruesome Lancashire legend — a priest who answers a spirit’s demand for “a body and a soul” with the body of a cock and the sole of a shoe — belongs to nineteenth‑century folklore, not to court records.
articles.summary: A gruesome Lancashire legend — a priest who answers a spirit’s demand for “a body and a soul” with the body of a cock and the sole of a shoe — belongs to nineteenth‑century folklore, not to court records.
articles.body:
The memorable trick — produce a cock’s body and a shoe’s sole, burn them and send the boggart packing — is the line that keeps the Clegg Hall story alive in the district. It’s vivid, comic and a touch grotesque; it is also a motif from folk-tale collections rather than a contemporaneous legal record. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/25256))

Clegg Hall itself is not fiction. The stone house on Clegg Hall Road, Little Clegg (near Milnrow) survives as a Grade II* listed building; its main fabric dates to the early seventeenth century and the National Heritage List entry records its architectural details and sources. The building was first listed on 10 August 1951. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

The tale as most readers expect it appears in Victorian folklore collections: a household is tormented by a “boggart” or household spirit said to be bound to the hall after a crime against children. When a priest is summoned and the spirit demands “a body and a soul,” the cleric produces a cock and the sole of a shoe, burns them and so lays the spirit — at least temporarily. This version is preserved in John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and in nineteenth‑century compilations that drew on Roby’s material. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/25256))

There is more than one way the story was told. Collectors printed dramatic variants and local ballads: William Nuttall of Rochdale supplied a ballad that elaborated characters and violence; county compilers quoted local proverbs that used the boggart’s name to mean something hard to get rid of. Those repeated tellings are useful evidence of how the story circulated and changed in speech and print. ([iapsop.com](https://iapsop.com/ssoc/1867__harland_wilkinson___lancashire_folk-lore.pdf))

When historians look for a contemporaneous crime to match Roby’s narrative they come up short. A late‑nineteenth‑century parish history that inventories local houses and families explicitly describes Roby’s account as “pure imagination” while acknowledging a ghost‑tradition and a local proverb — “As ill as Clegg Hall boggart” — that show the tale’s hold on local speech. There are no surviving court or parish records that confirm the dramatic murders narrated by folklorists. ([your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com](https://your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/04145039/chapter-xvii-old-houses-and-old-families-butterworth-pages337-389.pdf))

The cock‑and‑shoe bargain is not unique to Clegg Hall. Folklorists have long noted motifs in which a spirit demanding a body and soul is tricked with a bird’s body and an inanimate “soul” substitute; such formulas are part of a wider European folk repertoire that nineteenth‑century collectors drew on, adapted and localised. That diffusion helps explain why the image is so durable: it is cultural shorthand for outwitting a restless presence. ([readingroo.ms](https://readingroo.ms/4/8/1/2/48123/48123-h/48123-h.htm))

For readers who prefer facts to fable: the architectural and documentary record gives Clegg Hall a clear place in local history — its list entry cites the Victoria County History and a late‑nineteenth‑century parish account for owners, dates and structural description — but the lurid murder narrative is a product of oral tradition and Victorian compilation, not surviving trial papers. The place name, the proverb and the ballad verses are the evidence we have of the boggart’s cultural life. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

That leaves the Clegg Hall boggart where it belongs for most purposes: in folklore, not the record of criminal proceedings. The story is worth keeping — as an example of how a local proverb and a single telling can grow into a regional legend — but readers should treat the cock, the shoe and the priest as part of Lancashire storytelling rather than a literal local history. If you walk past Clegg Hall on a dull afternoon you may still hear the tale; just don’t expect to find the court papers that prove the dark centre of the story.

articles.title: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing updates on Representative Body developments
articles.excerpt: Andrew Johnson has been re-appointed as Chair of the RBH Representative Body, with Rachael Ray as Deputy Chair, as they work to improve services for residents.
articles.content_html:
Andrew Johnson has been re-appointed as Chair of the Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) Representative Body during a meeting held last week. He welcomed Rachael Ray as the new Deputy Chair and acknowledged the contributions of outgoing Deputy Chair Rob Dyson. This update was shared on October 27, 2026, and highlights the ongoing commitment of the Representative Body to enhance services for residents.

During the meeting, the Representatives approved RBH's Annual Report to Customers, which is available on the RBH website. Johnson expressed satisfaction that the Representatives were able to provide additional oversight before the report's publication.

The body also approved the findings of a recent scrutiny review aimed at improving customer feedback regarding the investment programme.

The scrutiny review resulted in six out of seven recommendations being accepted, including tailored approaches for gathering feedback from different customer groups.

Johnson thanked the panel members and RBH staff for their efforts in this review, which aims to enhance how the organisation interacts with its customers and manages services.

Membership in RBH allows residents to have a voice in shaping the services that affect their homes and communities.

Johnson encouraged those not yet members to sign up, emphasizing that their involvement strengthens the organisation and ensures it remains responsive to the needs of the community.

articles.title: Free benefits checks at Littleborough and Wardle libraries on Monday and Tuesday
articles.excerpt: Council advisers will offer free, no booking needed benefits checks at Littleborough Library on 26 October and Wardle Library on 27 October, from 10am to noon.
articles.content_html:
Residents unsure whether they are receiving all the financial support available to them can speak to council advisers at two free library drop in sessions this week. The sessions are particularly relevant to pensioners, carers, disabled residents and people worried about household costs, but the council says they are open to adults generally.

The first is at Littleborough Library in Hare Hill Park, Littleborough OL15 9HE, on Monday 26 October 2026 from 10am until noon. The second takes place at Wardle Library, 448 Birch Road, Wardle OL12 9LH, on Tuesday 27 October, also from 10am until noon. No appointment is needed for either event.

The council says advisers can check potential entitlement to Pension Credit, explain Attendance Allowance, review Council Tax Support eligibility and give information about Winter Fuel Payments, Blue Badge applications and other cost of living assistance. They can also signpost residents to organisations offering further help, including Citizens Advice and Age UK. Attending does not guarantee entitlement to a benefit or an immediate payment: decisions depend on the relevant eligibility rules and application process.

Anyone attending is asked to bring details of their income, pensions, savings and benefits already received, so advisers can offer a more accurate check. Those visiting on behalf of a family member should bring relevant information if available. Take care with personal documents and give sensitive details only to the advisers at the official session.

Both sessions are advertised by Rochdale Borough Council as free and do not require booking. Anyone unable to attend can use the council's published events information to find its contact details and check for other advice sessions.

Official event details: Littleborough Library https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/1484/pension-credit-awareness-drop-in-event---littleborough-library and Wardle Library https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/1485/pension-credit-awareness-drop-in-event---wardle-library.

articles.title: New book showcases unseen 1930s photographs of Rochdale's Norden Riviera
articles.excerpt: A new book featuring 600 unseen photographs captures the essence of 1930s Rochdale, including the lost Norden Riviera lido, highlighting the area's historical significance during a transformative decade.
articles.content_html:
A new book titled "Britain in the 1930s" by Steven Brindle and Maureen Hill features 600 previously unseen photographs, including images of Rochdale's lost Norden Riviera lido.

This collection captures the essence of Greater Manchester on the brink of World War II, showcasing the stark contrasts of the era.

The Norden Riviera, which opened in 1935, was a popular outdoor swimming pool located off Edenfield Road in Norden. It provided a seaside experience for local families who could not afford to travel far. The facility included diving boards, slides, and spectator stands, surrounded by gardens and sports fields, making it a cherished local attraction during the 1930s.

The book highlights the economic challenges faced by the north of England during this decade, with unemployment rates soaring due to the decline of traditional industries.

However, it also reflects a time of joy and resilience, as communities sought leisure and enjoyment amidst the hardships of the Great Depression and the aftermath of World War I.

"Britain in the 1930s" is available for £50 and covers various regions, including parts of the old Lancashire, now Greater Manchester. The inclusion of Rochdale's Norden Riviera serves to illustrate the area's rich history and the importance of preserving local heritage.

View 8 Images Cashier at the Ritz Dancing Hall. Manchester, on Boxing Day 1938 Add to preferred sources Comments News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 05:53, 26 Oct 2026 Storm clouds were gathering again globally. But on Boxing Day 1938 she captured, vivaciously, just one aspect of that decade. Crimson-lipped the cashier of the Ritz Dancing Hall in Manchester reflected the population's determination to find joy after the dark days of the First World War, the Great Depression, and unemployment. The 1930s led novelist and broadcaster JB Priestley to his famous vision of "three Englands" – the ancient country of cathedrals and villages, the blackened and scarred industrial Britain created by the Victorians, and the Americanised new consumer world of suburbs, cinemas and motorcars. He came to the conclusion after travelling the country with his suitcase and a typewriter to find material for his book "English Journey" published in 1934. ‌ Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter The decade in Britain saw a nation in transition. The north was hit hard by economic turmoil with unemployment levels soaring above the national average due to the collapse of industries like coal mining and shipbuilding. However, seaside cities became alive in the 1930s, thanks to the expansion of cheap rail travel and the emerging concept of paid holidays with thousands of working-class families flooding to the coast during their “Wakes Weeks” But the south and the midlands had seen a growth in new industries, notably car making, and electrical goods, and were able to withstand the economic fallout which the book says were distributed in a "grotesquely uneven way". ‌ A picture of a young, very well dressed couple, on Oxford Street, London, shows how affluence thrived in parts of the country while elsewhere, like the Lancashire George Orwell (pen name for Eric Blair) discovered in his travelogue "The Road to Wigan Pier" working class communities were decimated by the decline of traditional industries. View 8 Images A Wigan street decorated with washing, 1930s. The land as a place of marked contrasts is captured in a new book, Britain in the 1930s by Steven Brindle and Maureen Hill from Atlantic Publishing, price £50. It features 600 unseen black and white historic photographs of the UK. Counties covered by the book include parts of the old Lancashire, which are now in Greater Manchester, Cheshire, Yorkshire, Lancashire, and Northumberland. ‌ Images include an outdoor swimming pool in Rochdale in 1936 known as the Norden Riviera; soldiers clearing snow from the Manchester to Sheffield railway line; and a busy Deansgate in December 1930. A now lost Rochdale lido gave Mancunians a chance to enjoy a seaside experience without having to travel to the coast or abroad. The Norden Riviera opened in 1935 during when open air swimming was booming in Britaian. Located just off Edenfield Road in Norden, it was 'Rochdale by the sea' for many who could not afford a longer journey or who preferred something nearer to home. The pool was heated and came equipped with diving boards, slides and spectator stands. It was surrounded by attractive gardens, a cafe, a sports field with horse riding facilities, fences for show jumping, cricket pitches and areas for ball games. ‌ View 8 Images The "Rochdale Riviera" - the open air pool as it was at Norden in 1936. The Manchester Guardian newspaper on August 17, 1935. described the facility. It said: "The Norden pool, which measures 80ft by 40ft and is from 2ft 6in deep to 9ft deep is situated in the grounds of what, before the war, was Tenter House, just beyond the bleachworks at Norden, and the stables, where horses are kept for hire, belonged to this residence." "It is surrounded by green deckchairs and by an outdoor café, where one may have tea (or other meals) under green and yellow umbrellas. All around are delightful woods, beyond which one can see a shoulder of hill - but not the three factory chimneys lower down the valley. "A round paddling-pool satisfies the children too young to swim, and the conservatory of the old house has been turned into a ballroom. Next season, tennis courts, a gymnasium, a miniature golf course, and a children's playground will be added to the attractions of the Norden Riviera. ‌ View 8 Images A well-dressed couple in Oxford Street in 1932. "Bathing in the warmed water often continues till late by the light of powerful electric lamps." Other images in the book include Manchester's Cenotaph in St Peter's Square in 1935 in its original location before it was dismantled and reconstructed by Manchester City Council in 2014 at the northeast corner of the square next to the town hall to make way for the expansion of the Metrolink tram service. The memorial was first unveiled on July 12th 1924 by the Earl of Derby assisted by a Mrs Bingle, a local resident, whose three sons all died in the First World War. ‌ View 8 Images Manchester's Cenotaph in St Peter's Square pictured in 1935. A street in Wigan is pictured decorated with washing strung out across it. A Liverpool policeman directing traffic is seen standing in a protector box. These days the East Lancashire Road can be a notorious spot for traffic chaos. But a 1933 picture of the then "Liverpool to South East Lancashire Road" shows just eight vehicles over a half mile distance. The 27 mile highway was built at a cost of £3m. Britain was on the cusp of change in the 1930s. A world that would soon be transformed forever by the Second World War. ‌ Photographs in the book cover every county and city at that time, revealing a nation poised between tradition and modernity. articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards £1.1 million contract for young people's accommodation
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract worth over £1 million to Stepping Stone Projects for a new supported accommodation service for young people at risk of homelessness.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract valued at £1,108,081 to Stepping Stone Projects for the Rochdale Team Around the Young Person Accommodation Model (TAYPAS). This initiative aims to provide supported accommodation for young people aged 18 to 25 who are at risk of or experiencing homelessness. The contract will run from November 2, 2026, to November 1, 2029.

The TAYPAS model will deliver specialist, psychologically informed support within a newly developed, purpose-built facility that will feature 28 self-contained units. The service will offer 24/7 support and management, ensuring that young residents receive the assistance they need to transition into independent living.

This development is significant for the local community as it addresses the pressing issue of youth homelessness in Rochdale.

By providing a safe and supportive environment, the council aims to improve the life chances of vulnerable young people in the area, helping them to build skills and confidence.

The next steps involve the construction and operational setup of the accommodation, which is expected to be completed in the coming months. This initiative not only reflects the council's commitment to supporting young people but also highlights the importance of addressing homelessness in the borough.

articles.title: The Healey Dell prophecy: Eleanor Byron, Mother Bagden and what the records actually show
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.summary: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge — the Thrutch — is one of Rochdale borough’s most durable story‑places. The best‑known version of the tale says a local noblewoman, usually called Lady Eleanor (later linked by tellings to the Byron family), visited a fortune‑teller named Mother Bagden; the woman predicted Eleanor would be a maid, a wife and a widow all in one day, and on her wedding night the bridegroom was killed. That dramatic sequence appears in the earliest printed collections of Lancashire lore and in the Dell’s modern visitor material, but the story’s status changes sharply once you separate nineteenth‑century collectors from contemporary medieval records. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

The oldest printed witness we can point to is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire, a book of collected oral tales published in the early 1800s; Roby preserves a long, romance‑style narrative set at Healey that includes a miller, a ‘Fairies’ Chapel’, a talisman and the fatal wedding night that fulfils the prophecy. Roby’s purpose was to record local storytelling rather than to provide documentary proof of medieval events, and his account reads as literary folklore rather than archival history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Local antiquarians and guidebooks of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries amplified Roby’s version. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s trail guides and a short history leaflet reproduce the same outline: Ralph the miller, a messenger, Mother Bagden who claims intimate contact with a Fairy Queen, and the prediction that Eleanor will be “maid, wife and widow” in one day, followed by the death of her groom in a family feud. Those local guides attribute their narrative to older local histories such as William Robertson’s writings. The Heritage Centre presents the material as local myth and interpretation, alongside explanations of the Dell’s geology and industrial archaeology. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

What is demonstrably factual? Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve and visitor attraction at 121 Dell Road, with industrial archaeology (old mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Victorian railway viaduct that now forms part of a riverside trail. The viaduct is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those physical and administrative facts are public and documentable. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

What is folklore and what is missing from the archive? The supernatural elements — a Fairy Queen with prophetic power, spells that cause a bridegroom’s death, a named medieval Lady Eleanor whose wedding‑night fate is attested in contemporary court rolls or parish registers — lack contemporary documentary support. The story’s appearance in sources begins with nineteenth‑century collectors (Roby) and later local antiquarians (for example William Robertson as cited in modern guides); no contemporaneous medieval legal documents or parish entries confirming the prophecy or the precise characters named in the tale have been produced in those printed sources. In short: the prophecy belongs to the region’s oral and printed folklore tradition rather than to verified medieval record. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Why the story endures is straightforward: Healey Dell’s dramatic rock cleft, the Thrutch, looks for stories. A recess by the river invites the idea of a “Fairies’ Chapel”, and the valley’s history of mills, local rival families and visible ruins supplied the narrative scaffolding that collectors and guidebook writers later filled with characters and prophecy. The Heritage Centre explicitly treats the tale as part of the Dell’s storytelling — useful to visitors but not presented as archival fact. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

If you want to follow the trace yourself: read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed narrative; consult the Healey Dell Heritage Centre material for the local retelling and references to later antiquarians; and visit the Dell to see the viaduct, the Thrutch and the mill remains that inspired the story. If you hope to find a medieval legal record proving the prophecy, those proving documents are not cited in the early printed collectors and have not been produced in the local guides that preserve the tale — which is why historians and the Heritage Centre treat it as legend, however rooted in local memory it may be. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The tale of Lady Eleanor, Mother Bagden and the Fairies’ Chapel at Healey Dell is well attested in local printed collectors — but it survives as folklore, not as a documented medieval event.
articles.summary: The tale of Lady Eleanor, Mother Bagden and the Fairies’ Chapel at Healey Dell is well attested in local printed collectors — but it survives as folklore, not as a documented medieval event.
articles.body:
Ask a local where the Fairies’ Chapel is and they’ll point you down the steps from Station Road, into the ravine by the River Spodden. Ask whether fairies live there and the practical answer is simple: no verifiable evidence supports the existence of fairies; what the records do show is a named rock formation, a cluster of old stories collected in the nineteenth century and a long history of people visiting the site because the place feels, to many, a little uncanny. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

Those are not trivial facts. Healey Dell is a designated Local Nature Reserve and an area of industrial archaeology that straddles borough boundaries; part of the valley was legally made a statutory LNR in April 1976. The most dramatic built feature is the Healey Dell Viaduct, a high, eight‑arched sandstone railway viaduct that is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those designations are documentary and can be checked. ([rossendale.gov.uk](https://www.rossendale.gov.uk/download/meetings/id/4148/e2_appendix_2))

The Dell’s historical record is everyday, material and useful. The valley contains the remains of nineteenth‑century mills and the disused Rochdale‑to‑Bacup railway line; archaeological and conservation surveys catalogue those features and guide how the reserve is managed for wildlife and visitors. Management is led locally by Rochdale (and neighbouring Rossendale) authorities and by volunteer groups; published ecological reports and neighbourhood plans reference Healey Dell when mapping green infrastructure for the area. That is the part of the story that affects readers’ lives—path repairs, parking signage, listed‑building consent for the viaduct—because those are things the council, landowners and statutory consultees can change. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

The Fairies’ Chapel and the Healey Dwarf belong to a different archive: folklore. Nineteenth‑century writers and local collectors, notably the county antiquarian tradition and later local compilers, set down tales about a natural recess in the rock that looked a little like an altar and could be called a chapel. Early print references—quoted in modern guides—describe a hidden pulpit‑like formation revealed when a flood washed away a covering ledge; later colourful retellings add a Fairy Queen, a Fairy King and a bewitched dwarf or witch‑figure, motifs common to British fairy lore. Those stories come from literary and folkloric sources rather than parish registers, court records or archaeological excavation reports; they are valuable for what they tell us about local imagination and nineteenth‑century reading habits, not as evidence of the supernatural. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

You can still see the place‑name on the ground. Local walking leaflets and heritage trails mark a route down to the feature and signposts to a ‘Fairy Chapel’ appear on nearby footpaths and at the steps off Station Road. Community events and the Tearooms’ heritage material reproduce the old legends for visitors, which keeps the stories alive. None of these modern references change the distinction: a name, an attractive rock formation and repeated storytelling are not proof of otherworldly residents. ([whitworth.gov.uk](https://www.whitworth.gov.uk/uploads/walkingdocuments/files/WALK%206%20Healey%20Dell%20-%20captioned%20viaduct.pdf))

What remains uncertain—and worth noting—is provenance. Some of the best‑known versions of the Healey tales were shaped by nineteenth‑century collectors and local storytellers; when folklore circulates in print, oral tradition and tourism literature it can harden into ‘local history’ in popular memory. Where claims involve specific historical persons, dates or events, they should be tested against archival material; in the case of the Fairies’ Chapel, the archive records the place and the stories about it, not supernatural events. If you want proof, visit the council‑maintained reserve, look up the Historic England listing for the viaduct and read the nineteenth‑century sources for yourself—then decide whether the place’s atmosphere does the rest. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))
articles.content_html:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge, the Thrutch, has long been a place that invites stories.

Visitors still stand under the Victorian viaduct, follow the path to the small pool visitors call the Fairies’ Chapel, and hear the familiar local version: a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden prophesied that a noblewoman, usually named Lady Eleanor (later linked with the Byron family), would be a maiden, a wife and a widow in one day; on her wedding day the bridegroom was slain and the prophecy fulfilled.

That dramatic sequence is not a modern invention. The earliest printed form widely available to readers comes from the 19th century: John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire preserves a long, romance‑style account set at Healey that gives the tale its shape and characters. Later local antiquarians — notably William Robertson in his regional histories — recycled and amplified the narrative, and modern site interpretation at Healey Dell Heritage Centre follows that printed tradition when it tells visitors the Fairies’ Chapel story.

What is verifiable fact? Healey Dell is a named Local Nature Reserve and visitor attraction at Dell Road, with recognisable industrial archaeology (mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Grade II listed viaduct built for the Lancashire and Yorkshire extension railway in 1869–70. Those are public, documentable features you can still see. The Heritage Centre publishes its own guides that describe the gorge, the so‑called Fairies’ Chapel and the local legends; Rochdale Borough Council lists the reserve, its address, opening details and facilities. The viaduct is recorded on the National Heritage List for England. These are the things you can check on official records and by visiting.

What is folklore? The supernatural elements — a Fairy Queen who issues prophecies, a witch‑fortune‑teller who communes with her, or the idea that a named medieval Lady Eleanor’s fate is attested in contemporary legal or parish records — belong to oral tradition and antiquarian storytelling.

Roby, Robertson and later guide‑book writers recorded what people were telling in their own times rather than producing medieval documents. Local interpretation today openly presents the story as legend rather than as archival history.

How the story changed over time is itself revealing. Roby’s early 19th‑century text gives a literary, sometimes florid narrative with named characters: a miller, a talisman, Oliver Chadwyke and a Lady Eleanor.

Later retellings folded in local family names (Byron, Chadwick) and local topography (the Thrutch, the Fairies’ Chapel).

The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s material adapts those versions when it points visitors to the rock formation and to the flood of 1838 that altered the gorge and submerged some of the features said to be the ‘chapel’.

That lineage — oral tale into printed folklore into heritage interpretation — is a common path for many English place legends.

What cannot be shown from surviving records is the medieval documentary backbone the story implies.

I found no contemporary 15th‑century court rolls, parish registers or legal documents that confirm a wedding‑night killing, a named Lady Eleanor Byron of the period, or a recorded prophetic witch in Healey Dell.

Where claims cannot be matched to contemporary archives, the careful historian treats them as tradition and story. The result is not dismissal but classification: good material for local imagination, caution for anyone treating it as proven history.

If you want to see the story’s sources for yourself: read John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed tale, inspect the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s guide for the way the tale is now presented on site, and consult Rochdale Borough Council and the National Heritage List for England for the reserve’s practical and architectural facts.

The prophecy endures because place, geology and a few dramatic printed versions make for memorable storytelling. That is a valuable local inheritance — so long as readers keep legend and archive in separate pockets.

Practical details: Healey Dell Nature Reserve and the Heritage Centre are listed by Rochdale Borough Council (address Dell Road, Healey). The viaduct is Grade II listed on Historic England’s National Heritage List.

For maps, opening times and the Heritage Centre’s explanatory leaflets, use the council and the centre’s published material.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council invites feedback on proposed Customer Access strategy
articles.excerpt: Residents are encouraged to share their views on the proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy, which aims to enhance how the public interacts with the Council over the next five years.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has launched a consultation inviting residents to provide feedback on its proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy for the next five years. The strategy aims to simplify how residents contact the Council and ensure they receive consistent support, whether online, by phone, or in person.

The Council has identified six priorities for enhancing customer access and nine pledges detailing what residents can expect from the service. The aim is to create a seamless experience for users, allowing them to receive assistance without needing to navigate the Council's organisational structure.

The Council emphasises the importance of making it easy for individuals to access the right help, especially during challenging times.

Residents can review the draft strategy and related documents, including the Equality Impact Assessment and Sustainability Impact Assessment, on the Council's consultation hub. The Council is keen to know if the proposed priorities resonate with the community and whether any aspects have been overlooked.

The consultation documents are available for review and can be accessed through the Council's website.

The consultation is open now, and residents are encouraged to participate to help shape the final version of the strategy. Feedback can be submitted through the Council's website until the consultation period closes.

This initiative represents an opportunity for the community to influence how the Council interacts with its residents over the coming years.

articles.title: Residents face uncertainty as Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks undergo safety review
articles.excerpt: The future of Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks remains uncertain as residents prepare to relocate amid safety concerns and ongoing housing limbo.
articles.content_html:
Residents of Rochdale's College Bank estate, known for its iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks, are facing significant uncertainty as they prepare to move out due to safety concerns. The landowners, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH), informed 229 households in October 2025 that they would need to vacate the premises. Currently, only about 90 households remain in the blocks, with many residents already relocated as part of a safety review process.

Claire Lord, a long-term resident of the Mardyke block, expressed her reluctance to leave her home, citing the security and community she has enjoyed for over a decade.

She is currently waiting for a move to a nearby bungalow, but delays in renovations have left her without a confirmed moving date.

Claire's situation reflects the broader anxiety among residents, many of whom are concerned about losing their established support networks and the uncertainty surrounding the future of the tower blocks.

The safety review has raised questions about whether the blocks will be demolished or refurbished, with no clear timeline provided by RBH. Residents have reported receiving conflicting information about the future of their homes, leading to a climate of speculation and concern.

Christine Hartley, another resident, is still awaiting a suitable replacement for her two-bedroom flat, which she fears may not be possible due to the size constraints of available options.

As the situation develops, the local community is left grappling with the implications of these changes. The uncertainty surrounding the Seven Sisters highlights the ongoing challenges of housing safety and the need for clear communication from housing authorities.

Residents are encouraged to maintain regular contact with RBH for updates on their housing situation.
