evidence_sources.captured_text: The secret safety battle over Rochdale’s Seven Sisters - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news The secret safety battle over Rochdale’s Seven Sisters SPECIAL REPORT: As clutter boxes pile high in the living rooms of the 90 remaining households on Rochdale's College Bank estate, an M.E.N. investigation uncovers BSR building safety notices, £1.7m empty council tax bills, and the human cost of a decade-long housing limbo. George Lythgoe reports. View 7 Images Town Mill Brow tower block on College Bank with a wonky R (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) Add to preferred sources Comments News George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter and Stephen Topping Senior reporter 07:07, 25 Oct 2026 Claire Lord sits alone in her living room surrounded by head-high boxes. The small space between her sofa and TV is the only bit of the flat not crowded by cubes of clutter. To answer the door she has to clamber over yet more plastic tubs filled to the brim with her worldly possessions. The 56-year-old is ready to move out of her flat in Rochdale ’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks. She’s been ready for weeks. ‌ Claire was one of 229 households told they had to leave by landowners Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) in October 2025. Since then, droves have been moving out of the blocks. Only an estimated 90 households are still left in Seven Sisters - actually named College Bank. RBH says this has been done for safety reasons. View 7 Images College Bank tower blocks in Rochdale known as the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) The tower blocks face an uncertain future, with the question of demolition or refurbishment still on the table after a decade of limbo. No matter the decision, it is understood all residents will have to move out whilst work is done - whether that work is to decorate or destroy. ‌ Claire is one of the latest to be exiting the estate, but it’s not a move she really wanted to do. When describing the day when RBH told her they'd found some new digs for her, she said she was ‘gutted’. The security, the views, proximity to healthcare professionals and the community are the things she cherishes most about her flat. Claire will be moving to a bungalow across the road, behind Lidl. “There has been a delay because the lady who lived in the bungalow hadn't done work on the place for some time,” Claire explained. “They’ve had to do painting and decorating, rewiring, putting new doors on and a fresh kitchen. ‌ “So they’ve been getting it ready for me. RBH told me about four months ago that I’d be moving and were waiting for the date. “Every time I’ve gone down they’ve come up with more work and more work to do. I’ve been down every week to ask. “It’s always the same story - ‘something is being done’. I’ve still not got a move-in date, I think I’ll be told about a move-in date in four weeks. “I do love living here. The security is good and there isn’t much chance of you getting burgled. ‌ “It’s close to the shops in the town centre, my mental health team is nearby and my GP is just down the road. “But my biggest fear of moving is losing that security. I’ve been here (in Mardyke block) for 12 years and I've never had any trouble, it’s a good community. “If I could stay I would. It’s not good for my mental health. I don’t know whether I’m coming or going. “Being stuck halfway is no good as I just don’t know. They’re just going to plonk a day on me.” ‌ View 7 Images Claire Lord, Mardyke resident on the Seven Sisters estate in Rochdale (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) Claire has credited RBH with supporting her through the transition. She has regular contact with housing officers, but that doesn’t mean the transition process has been easy for her. Like many of the tenants, she just wants to know what’s happening with the blocks. Claire added: “We’ve had so many rumours about what is happening. We’ve heard they’re bringing in migrants in; that three are staying up and four are coming down; then we’ve had that they’re all staying up; then we’ve had they’re all coming down and they’re building 250 houses. ‌ “Nothing is set in concrete and they won’t tell us. It’s all just rumours.” Her friend Christine Hartley, who has lived in the Tentercroft block for 14 years, hasn’t accepted any new accommodation from RBH. She is still waiting on a 'like for like replacement', which she admits isn’t really possible due to the size of her two-bed flat. The 67-year-old said: "You know there is someone you can rely on in the blocks. We often ring each other, pop in and check on each other as there are loads of people that have known each other for years. “When we were fighting the campaign, you’d nip to the shop and an hour later you’d get hope because so many people would stop us to ask what is happening with the flats. We’re still getting that now. ‌ “It’s a good question. What is happening with the flats? I'd ask RBH. “They sent a letter last week saying they’ve still not made a decision. But I think they have made a decision, but they just don’t want us to know what it is. “Why should we have to move out when they won’t tell us what they’re doing with the flats? It doesn’t make sense. “You can’t tell me they don’t know what they’re doing. It wouldn’t be the case if they didn’t let them get into this state. ‌ “It’s very quiet on the estate now, even during the day. It never used to be like this, it used to be bustling.” “Why can’t they just tell us what they’re doing? It’s more than due time to tell us now. “We’ve suffered long enough and it plays with your mental health. I’ve cried, I’ve been angry. “Just give us a bit of truth, we deserve that. We deserve some respect, it’s ridiculous.” ‌ View 7 Images College Bank tower blocks in Rochdale known as the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) This is a fair question to ask if you’re being forced to leave your home. Although a number of former College Bank residents have expressed their happiness with the new digs sorted for them by RBH. Christine and her partner Roy Kitcher thought their Tentercroft flat was going to be their forever home. They love life on Seven Sisters and see no reason to move. Speaking on why he is adamant on staying, Roy told the M.E.N : “We moved in here and we were at risk of becoming homeless. We thought this was going to be forever. We love it here. ‌ “It’s right next to the town centre, the doctors are down the road, the chemist is down the road. It’s spacious and we have everything we need right here. Why should we have to move? “When people move out of here RBH are getting reduced rates to move. Those are going to go up and people who’ve moved out could get into dire straits. “When we’re coming back from the holiday or a trip to the lighthouse, I point at the blocks and say ‘home’s over there’. Or coming down the motorway, as soon as I see the Seven Sisters, we’re almost homes now. “Before I moved in I told people I would never move into College Bank, because I didn’t like the look of them. Moving in changed my mind.” The pair are both part of the Save the Seven Sisters (ST7S) campaign that has been going ever since the intention to demolish came knocking. They feel like RBH is disrespecting residents by not explaining why they have to move, or showing the findings of the surveys that sparked the mass exodus in October 2025. ‌ There has been a long history of mistrust between tenants and their landlord, which goes back over a decade. The Manchester Evening News first reported on the possibility of the Seven Sisters being bulldozed by RBH in November 2016. At the time, the housing provider said it would consider proposals for College Bank and Lower Falinge the following spring ‘at the earliest’. RBH spoke of ‘reduced demand for flats as a result of recent welfare reforms’. But in the 10 years since, the picture has changed dramatically. According to Greater Manchester Combined Authority’s (GMCA) housing market monitor, 43 per cent of the 7,892 households on Rochdale’s active social housing register required a one-bedroom property in 2024-25, while 29 per cent needed a two-bedroom property. Campaigners argue that College Bank’s roughly 670 empty flats would make a significant dent in that waiting list. ‌ View 7 Images College Bank tower blocks in Rochdale known as the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) Plans unveiled by RBH in June 2017 would have seen four of the Seven Sisters towers knocked down - Mitchell Hey, Dunkirk Rise, Tentercroft and Town Mill Brow - to make way for up to 120 new homes. The three remaining blocks would have been modernised. Demolition notices were handed out to tenants in March 2019 , but residents refused to give up their homes without a fight. Rochdale councillors and then-mayor Andy Burnham also raised concerns , with local politicians going on to step up their scrutiny of RBH in the years to come. In 2020, a tragedy elsewhere in Rochdale that would bring national scrutiny to RBH and send shockwaves across the country. Awaab Ishak, who lived in a flat on the Freehold estate with his mum and dad, died aged two in December 2020. ‌ His parents had made repeated requests for help with a damp and mould issue at their home, but the issue was not properly addressed. Coroner Joanne Kearsley ruled that exposure to mould at the flat led to Awaab’s death, as she described the tragedy as a ‘defining moment’ for the housing sector . Before Awaab’s inquest took place, an M.E.N investigation in summer 2022 revealed that issues of damp and mould were widespread on the Freehold estate . Other families reported having children with breathing difficulties while living in the same conditions that Awaab’s family faced. The scandal sparked the successful campaign for Awaab’s Law , while RBH went on to be downgraded by the regulator and had their ability to generate private funding frozen. Gareth Swarbrick, the chief executive who had overseen plans to knock down the Seven Sisters, initially refused to resign before being ousted by the social landlord’s board in November 2022 . His interim replacement, Yvonne Arrowsmith, signalled a new era for the beleaguered housing provider. In March 2023, RBH announced a review into the plans for College Bank, before Ms Arrowsmith told the M.E.N in June 2023 that the landlord hoped to save the tower blocks from demolition . ‌ The social landlord entered into an exclusivity agreement with Legal and General Affordable Homes to ‘explore alternative options’, including a full refurbishment of all seven towers. But in October 2024, one year after Amanda Newton had taken over as RBH chief executive, the exclusivity agreement came to an end - with demolition brought back to the table . Andy Burnham launched a mayoral taskforce in an attempt to raise funds for the refurbishment of the Seven Sisters the following month. The Greater Manchester Mayor was joined on that taskforce by strategic partners such as the local council, people from the housing industry, tenants union and political representatives. Housing and regeneration boss at Rochdale council , Coun Danny Meredith, said: “We remain fully committed to our involvement in the taskforce, and with a new Mayor of Greater Manchester now in post, we can continue the joint work that began under the previous Mayor. “Rochdale is still in a housing emergency, and as the council is not a housing stock–holding authority, we must rely on RBH and our partners to build new homes and bring existing stock back into use. ‌ “Right now, 363 households, including 245 families, are living in temporary accommodation. Many of these families have been waiting years for a permanent home. This is not sustainable, and it is not acceptable during a housing emergency. “This is why resolving the situation at Seven Sisters and Lower Falinge is absolutely critical. Across those sites, more than 800 homes currently stand empty. Unlocking those homes is one of the single biggest steps we can take to reduce the pressure on temporary accommodation and give residents the stability they deserve. “We need a clear, deliverable plan from RBH for these sites so that residents can finally have a home for life. I hope we can reach a resolution soon because residents of Rochdale Borough cannot afford further delay.” View 7 Images Mark Slater, campaign organiser for Save the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) ‌ Mark Slater has been a leading figure in the ST7S campaign group since its inception and is a member of the taskforce, now chaired by new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig. He feels that RBH have deliberately overseen the degradation of the blocks - what he described as ‘managed decline’. Mark said: “I am frustrated to the point of anger that we’ve got a situation where we are listening to RBH saying no decision has been made. But everything is pointing towards a decision under the radar and proceeding with a demolition agenda. “We’re speaking to colleagues, residents and tenants who are also concerned. We’ve lived with this since 2016 and have this Sword of Damocles dangling over our heads. “For whatever reason RBH have decided to go down a route of ‘lets find out a reason for them to be demolished. That’s the way it feels for people on the estate. ‌ “I’m sure Bev Craig will be looking at those comparisons with an emphasis on retaining social housing and building social housing. Those will be scrutinised very closely. “For an organisation to say ‘we’re transparent, we want to communicate, listen to what people are saying’ but they give us this story that the flats aren’t safe. But some people have lived here for decades. “We know they’ve suffered from the managed decline RBH have pursued with these blocks. It seems to us they’re using these surveys to justify an agenda of demolition.” RBH have vehemently denied this accusation on numerous occasions. The social housing provider has repeatedly claimed they are committed to supporting all residents in their transitions from the 1960s blocks. ‌ In Mark Slater’s eyes, money has been the driving force behind RBH’s decision making this whole time. Because of the way funding works in social housing, it is much easier to get government funding for building projects in social housing as opposed to retrofit. Homes England focus mainly on housebuilding rather than refurbishment projects, which would mean going to the private market for funding in the case of refurbishment of the Seven Sisters. For RBH, that was not an option for a long time due to them being placed in special measures back in 2022 in the wake of Awaab Ishak’s death, who lived on the Freehold estate also operated by RBH. Being put in special measures meant RBH had a freeze on funding in the private sector, therefore unable to fund a potential refurbishment project at College Bank. Mark added: “As far as housing is concerned, one of the things Andy Burnham said at the Labour Conference was looking at giving councils powers to repossess homes that have been kept empty for a period of time. We are pressing for details on that and to see if there is any potential we could use that policy decision to do what we need to do on College Bank. ‌ “Everyone is talking about the need to build social housing, but we’re not looking for solutions in estates like this. We are looking at reasons to demolish and it just doesn’t make sense. “Ever since 2016 one of the things that hundreds of people have asked is ‘why do they need to demolish them’. The reason is because there is funding available for new build projects, but no funding available for refurbishments. “That, in one fell swoop, could change the whole process. If Homes England could produce money for refurbishmentment, I would be very interested to see whether RBH could take advantage of that.” Hannah Fleming, director of regeneration and asset improvement at Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, said: “We have been transparent with our customers that the long-term safety of the buildings in their current state cannot be confirmed, and that any solution would require all customers to move out for at least a decade. ‌ “In the meantime, our focus remains on supporting our customers into their new homes. We have already made significant progress, with just under 90 households left to find their new home and most customers already settled in their new homes. “We are working individually with each household to ensure their move is as simple and straightforward as it possibly can be. We know that this is a significant change for many customers and we are working with each household individually to find them a home that meets their needs and requirements. “In some cases, the new homes have required additional work from our empty homes team before they are ready for our customer to move in. Where this is the case, our team keeps our customers fully informed and supported throughout.” View 7 Images Tentercroft residents Roy Kitcher and his partner Christine Hartley (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) ‌ When to expect a decision on the future of the blocks? A decision on the future of the Seven Sisters has been up in the air ever since demolition was put back on the table in 2024 - when the new regime at RBH came in. The social housing provider say they have conducted surveys that suggest there are a number of structural issues with the blocks and have costed up options for various forms of refurbishments and also demolition. Despite the surveys being completed near the end of 2025, no decision was made by RBH. It is understood that the taskforce designed to shape the future of Seven Sisters, created by former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham, wasn’t allowed full access to the surveys. So the taskforce agreed with RBH to have an independent review of the surveys. It is understood this was part of due diligence from a local authority point of view, with Rochdale council, Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), the tenants union and the local MP represented on the taskforce. ‌ The findings from that review are expected to be produced in the coming weeks and will be presented to the next taskforce meeting. After that, a decision on the future of the blocks will be made by RBH, but the taskforce will get a say in the matter. It is clear that all parties want to find a solution and have a decision. Campaigners claim that RBH have pushed the managed decline of the blocks in order to pursue demolition; the cost on RBH to keep so many flats empty is eyewatering. RBH have admitted it costs them £1.7m every year in council tax payments. The cost is astronomical because council tax bills increase the longer a property is empty. ‌ Empty homes council tax multipliers range from 100 per cent of the standard bill (double) in the first year, up to 300 per cent after five years of being empty and 400 per cent after 10 years of being empty. RBH executive Ms Fleming added: “It’s important that we make the right decision on the future of College Bank; not necessarily the fastest decision. Our focus throughout has been on doing the right thing for current and future customers, ensuring we can provide safe, warm, affordable homes that meet housing needs for generations to come. “The length of time this has taken reflects our commitment to working with our partners, as well as the complexity of the decision and the need to consider detailed surveys. As part of that process, Rochdale Borough Council and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority commissioned an independent review of the evidence, and we will discuss the findings of that work with partners before the RBH Board makes a decision on the future regeneration route for College Bank.” Rochdale MP Paul Waugh said: “Tenants have been left in limbo for far too long and I hope that they can be given the answers they need about the safety and the future of their homes. ‌ "I urge RBH to act as swiftly as possible to bring this to a conclusion on behalf of all Rochdale residents during a housing emergency. Each day these flats are left empty is another missed opportunity to support the many thousands of Rochdalians living in temporary or unsuitable accommodation. "The council and GMCA have confirmed their commitment to resolving this longstanding and emotive issue, and I will continue to work with colleagues across government to ensure the best quality housing in Rochdale is realised." The latest findings on the tower blocks’ structural integrity In summer 2020, extensive investigations on properties at College Bank uncovered serious problems with ‘compartmentation’ at Seven Sisters flats, which is supposed to prevent fire from spreading between apartments. RBH says a 24-hour waking watch was introduced as a result, plus bespoke fire alarm and evacuation alarm systems. Since then, the Building Safety Regulator (BSR) issued enforcement notices against RBH on four of the tower blocks - Dunkirk Rise, Mitchell Hey, Tentercroft and Town Mill Brow. ‌ In the notices, issued last summer and seen by the M.E.N following the release of documents under the Freedom of Information Act, the BSR said the landlord had failed to ‘take proportionate measures to manage the risk of spread of fire created by compartmentation issues’. Months later, Seven Sisters residents were told they would need to leave . Last October, RBH cited safety concerns regarding structural and electrical issues, problems with the water pumping system, roof damage and increasing costs to heat and light the properties as reasons for the move. The Mitchell Hey block was then evacuated in March 2026 , when a water pipe burst. Campaigners - backed by Rochdale councillors - say they are still yet to see the concrete evidence of why they need to leave the College Bank flats. A spokesperson for the Save the Seven Sisters campaign said: “Despite numerous requests by residents, campaigners and local politicians, RBH still refuse to share any surveys they claim show potential long term safety issues requiring the blocks to be emptied. RBH have pushed to clear the estate of residents since October 2025, all while still claiming that no long term decision on the future of the estate has been made.” ‌ In the meantime, RBH has communicated its concerns over the Seven Sisters to the BSR. Correspondence released under the Freedom of Information Act, seen by the M.E.N, said: “Surveys have identified that although the buildings are currently safe, there are a number of issues which will deteriorate over time. This deterioration means that the long-term safety of the buildings in their current state cannot be confirmed as the issues with building repairs and condition are becoming more pressing as they continue to age. “We have therefore been closely considering the options for how we address this in the short to medium term, as any refurbishment option will take a number of years to plan and commence, and an estimated 12 years to complete across all seven buildings. We are fully cognisant of our duty to keep the buildings and our residents safe during that time, and also to protect the well-being of those residents and their quality of life.” After the M.E.N was given sight of the documents released by the BSR, Siobhan McCoy, director of property services at RBH, said: “The safety of our customers is our absolute priority. We wrote to all College Bank customers about these notices when they were first issued by the BSR more than a year ago, setting out what they meant and offering opportunities for people to speak directly with us. We also posted copies of the notices within each of the buildings together with information on safety and how to contact us about concerns. "The notices concerned ongoing structural surveys and a historic fire safety issue linked to refurbishment work carried out in the 1990s. This issue was identified by RBH in 2020 and a range of additional safety measures were put in place, including a 24-hour waking watch, bespoke fire alarm and evacuation alarm systems, and support for any customers who may need assistance in an emergency. ‌ "We have continued to work constructively with regulatory agencies to manage building safety risks and address regulatory requirements.The decision to rehouse our customers was informed by a range of factors, including structural investigations, the scale of the works that will be required in all regeneration scenarios and - primarily – customer safety. articles.title: East Lancashire Railway secures portable defibrillator for its trains
articles.excerpt: The heritage railway serving Heywood plans to take lifesaving equipment onboard and is seeking support for more mobile units.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has secured a portable defibrillator that will eventually travel on its trains, bringing potentially lifesaving equipment closer to passengers, staff and volunteers.

The heritage railway, which serves Heywood, received the Automated External Defibrillator (AED) following fundraising led by ELR Fund Raising Lead Adrian Dewey with support from national charity AEDdonate.

The unit is intended to move with train services rather than remain at a fixed location. It has not yet entered operational service. The railway says it will first establish arrangements for governance, asset management, equipment checks, training and deployment so it can be managed safely as it moves between services.

The new equipment will complement defibrillators already located at stations. ELR hopes to secure further mobile units, with the longer term ambition of extending coverage across all its operating services.

Chairman Mike Kelly said: “Keeping staff, volunteers and our visitors safe is our top priority. I want to thank AEDdonate for their timely donation and all of our kind donors for making this possible.”

He said having equipment available on trains, in addition to station defibrillators, would further strengthen the railway’s health and safety arrangements.

Phillip Warren, ELR Commercial Services Director and AED sponsor, said: “This is about putting lifesaving equipment where our passengers, volunteers and staff actually are.”

He explained that passengers may be travelling somewhere along the line rather than sitting beside a station building, making a portable unit an important additional resource in an onboard emergency.

“Hopefully this equipment will never be needed, but if that day ever comes, we want to have done everything reasonably possible to be prepared,” he said.

The announcement comes during Restart a Heart activity this October. The annual initiative, led by Resuscitation Council UK, promotes awareness of cardiac arrest and CPR education, with Restart a Heart Day held on 16 October.

As a registered charity, ELR relies on fundraising, donations, volunteers and support from businesses and other organisations. It is now inviting individuals to contribute to the next phase of the mobile AED project and businesses to consider sponsoring equipment.

Medical suppliers and other organisations able to donate a unit are also being encouraged to contact the railway.

Warren said: “It is a very tangible way of supporting a charity and potentially helping to save a life.”

Donations towards additional mobile defibrillators can be made through the ELR fundraising campaign: https://www.justgiving.com/campaign/elr-defibrilator-fundraiser

articles.title: Jolly Josh Christmas Ball sells out as Rochdale businesses urged to help
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is asking businesses to sponsor a table for £50 or donate raffle and auction prizes ahead of its December ball at Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh has filled the guest tables for its Jolly Jingle Christmas Ball and is now asking local businesses to help turn a full room into vital funding for families.

The ball takes place at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 11 December at 7pm. With guest places filled, the charity is inviting businesses across Rochdale and Greater Manchester to sponsor tables for £50, donate raffle or auction prizes, or discuss other ways to support the evening.

A contribution does not have to be extravagant. Vouchers, meals, products, experiences and services can all help boost the fundraising total.

Based at Ensor Mill on Queensway in Castleton, Jolly Josh says it supports more than 300 families of children and young people with complex medical needs, physical disabilities, life limiting conditions, and profound and multiple learning disabilities.

Its purpose built centre offers hydrotherapy, rebound therapy, sensory activities, youth social groups, accessible after school provision and support for parents and carers.

The charity says it receives no regular government funding, making grants, donations, community fundraising and business support essential to keeping its services running.

Rose Hutchings, Lead Fundraiser at Jolly Josh, said:

“We’ve been absolutely delighted by the response to this year’s Jolly Jingle Ball and to see the tables fill. What we’d really love now is for the wider Rochdale business community to help us make the night as successful as possible for our families.

“A £50 table sponsorship or a donated raffle or auction prize might feel like a relatively small contribution to a business, but when lots of local organisations get behind us those contributions quickly add up.

“Jolly Josh doesn’t receive regular government funding, so fundraising and community support genuinely help us continue providing a safe, accessible place where children and young people with complex needs and their families can connect, access opportunities and feel part of a community.”

The appeal comes as demand for the charity’s specialist services continues to grow. Jolly Josh says its hydrotherapy provision has previously run at least 42 sessions a week and experienced waiting lists, with strong demand for other services too.

Businesses interested in a £50 table sponsorship, donating a raffle or auction prize, or offering other event support can email Rose Hutchings at rose@jollyjosh.co.uk or call 01706 399141.

Further information about Jolly Josh, registered charity number 1178116, is available at https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

articles.title: Rochdale Sleep Out raises funds for homeless support
articles.excerpt: Fundraisers gathered at Crown Oil Arena for the annual Sleep Out, raising awareness and funds for homelessness initiatives in the community.
articles.content_html:
Fundraisers spent a night outdoors at Rochdale's Crown Oil Arena to raise awareness and vital funds for people experiencing homelessness. This event, the second annual Sleep Out organised by Petrus Communities and RAFC Community Trust, saw supporters from across the borough come together for a common cause.

The money raised will support the Changing Lives initiative, a football programme designed to assist individuals facing homelessness or living in supported accommodation.

The initiative aims to enhance participants' mental health, physical well-being, and social inclusion through free football sessions, while also providing personal development opportunities, including pathways into volunteering, education, and employment.

Louise Scriven, Fundraising and Partnerships Coordinator at Petrus, emphasised that the Sleep Out is not about pretending to experience homelessness, but about standing in solidarity with those facing housing insecurities. She noted that last year's event significantly impacted participants, helping them rebuild confidence, forge new friendships, and develop skills to become active community members.

The funds raised from this year's Sleep Out will continue to provide essential accommodation, support, advice, and opportunities for those experiencing homelessness and disadvantage in Rochdale, Oldham, and Burnley.

Donations are crucial for sustaining these services and making a difference in the lives of vulnerable individuals in the community.

articles.title: Broadfield Park Slopes renovation celebrated at Rochdale Town Hall
articles.excerpt: A special event at Rochdale Town Hall recognised the contributions of volunteers and partners involved in the restoration of Broadfield Park Slopes, highlighting the project's community impact and heritage significance.
articles.content_html:
A celebration was held at Rochdale Town Hall to honour the individuals and groups who contributed to the renovation of Broadfield Park Slopes.

This historic site, located between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church, has undergone significant restoration, thanks to the efforts of local volunteers and funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The event, organised by Polly Brant, Cultural Engagement Officer for Rochdale Council, brought together volunteers, partners, and community members to acknowledge their roles in the project. Guests were treated to a series of films by local filmmaker Jack Grindrod, showcasing the stories and heritage associated with the park's transformation. The films captured the community involvement that played a crucial role in the renovation process.

The evening featured poetry readings by Alende Amisi, a local poet and former young poet in residence, who shared his personal reflections on Rochdale's heritage.

His contributions added a personal touch to the event, which celebrated not only the park's restoration but also the community spirit that drove the project forward.

The renovation has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, and introduced new heritage interpretation.

The lower lawn has been terraced to create a natural amphitheatre, providing a new space for activities and events, enhancing the park's role as a community hub.

The celebration, arranged by Polly Brant, Rochdale Council Cultural Engagement officer, brought together volunteers, partners and people who have been involved in the project to recognise what has been achieved and, importantly, the contribution local people have made along the way. The Grade II listed Broadfield Park Slopes sit between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church and have been restored through a project delivered by Rochdale Development Agency working with Rochdale Borough Council, with funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund. Excavations have uncovered the footings of Charles Kershaw’s 19th century Central Corn Mill, cobbled trackways and the former public weigh station, alongside finds including ceramics, clay smoking pipes, animal bones and glass bottles. Four archaeological digs have taken place, with the wider programme involving schoolchildren, students, volunteers and members of the public. It has included 28 work placement students, 12 archaeological volunteers and a two year schools programme involving 715 pupils. Cllr Sue Smith, portfolio holder for Communities and Co-operation at Rochdale Council, said: “This was a wonderful opportunity to celebrate not just the transformation of the Broadfield Park Slopes, but the people who have made this project so special. “Our volunteers deserve a huge thank you. We have protected an important part of our heritage, opened it back up for people to enjoy and, crucially, involved our communities in doing it.” The Broadfield Park Slopes are now open to the public, creating a restored green space at the heart of Rochdale’s historic town centre. articles.title: Rochdale Council celebrates achievements of over 200 cared-for children at annual awards
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council hosted its annual awards ceremony at Matthew Moss High School, recognising the achievements of more than 200 cared-for children with medals and a day of entertainment.

The day included a variety of entertainment, such as trampolines, funfair rides, and face painting, allowing families to create joyful memories together.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, expressed her pride in the achievements of the children, stating, "They are all exceptional young people and show phenomenal determination to be their very best. This doesn’t go unnoticed by those around them."

The event aimed to provide public recognition for the hard work and accomplishments of these young individuals.

Local businesses sponsored the celebration, contributing to the activities and entertainment provided for families. Notable sponsors included A&T Surfacing Ltd, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, and Rochdale Hornets, among others. This community support helped create a memorable day for the children and their families.

articles.title: Jolly Josh welcomes Rochdale families with inclusive play, music and activity sessions
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with weekly sessions and bookable activities.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with a programme of inclusive activities and support.

Based at 2 Ensor Mill in Castleton, Rochdale, OL11 2NU, the centre welcomes children and young adults aged from birth to 19.

The charity says finding activities where a child is welcomed, understood and supported can be difficult, and wants more parents, carers, relatives and professionals to know what is available.

Its programme includes music and signing, themed play sessions, an after-school club, a youth group and activities that families can book directly with the centre.

Weekly sessions

Sing And Sign runs every Wednesday from 10.30am to 12.30pm, bringing together music, songs and signing to make communication fun.

Themed Stay And Play takes place every Tuesday and Saturday from 9.30am to 12.30pm. Sessions offer activities, friendship and a different theme each week.

Sensory Touch And Music runs every Thursday from 10am to noon, offering a relaxing sensory session.

articles.title: Future of College Bank towers uncertain as renovation could take over a decade
articles.excerpt: Housing chiefs have stated that renovating the College Bank tower blocks would displace residents for more than ten years, with no decision yet made on their future.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has confirmed that no decision has been made regarding the future of the College Bank tower blocks, known locally as the Seven Sisters. However, housing officials have warned that any renovation of the iconic structures would require residents to vacate their homes for over a decade.

The Seven Sisters, which have stood for 61 years, are in urgent need of modernisation. Residents have been advocating for refurbishment rather than demolition, and recently appealed to Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig for support in their campaign.

If the renovation proceeds, RBH has indicated that the buildings would not be habitable until the extensive work is completed.

The discussion around the future of College Bank began in 2017 when RBH expressed concerns about the buildings nearing the end of their lifespan.

In response, tenants formed the Save the Seven Sisters campaign, hoping that a partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would lead to restoration. However, in September 2024, it was announced that this partnership would not continue, prompting further calls for assistance from local leaders.

In November 2024, a Mayoral Taskforce was established to explore options for the College Bank estate. Following safety surveys conducted in October 2025, RBH declared that the blocks were unsafe for occupancy, necessitating the relocation of residents.

As the situation develops, the community awaits clarity on the next steps for the future of their homes.

articles.title: Springhill Hospice to host free will information clinic in Heywood
articles.excerpt: Springhill Hospice is offering a free information clinic for those looking to make or update their wills, with expert guidance available.
articles.content_html:
Springhill Hospice will hold a free information clinic aimed at individuals considering making or updating their wills.

The event will take place at the hospice, providing an opportunity for attendees to learn about the importance of having a will and to ask questions regarding the process.

David Copeland, a solicitor from Molesworths Solicitors based in Rochdale, will lead the session. Participants will receive a free will template and refreshments will be provided.

The clinic is designed for anyone, whether they are making their first will or looking to amend an existing one.

Charlotte Mascarenhas, supporter engagement fundraiser at Springhill Hospice, emphasised that the clinic aims to simplify the process of formalising a will, which can often feel daunting for many.

Molesworths Solicitors will waive their usual fees for this service, requesting only a donation to the hospice in return. Springhill Hospice offers care for adults with life-limiting conditions and support for their families across Heywood, Middleton, and Rochdale.

The clinic is open to the public, and there is no obligation to engage further services. Those interested in attending are encouraged to reach out to Springhill Hospice for more details.

articles.title: QTS Group hosts first safety Jamboree in Rochdale with over 350 attendees
articles.excerpt: The QTS Group's inaugural safety Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale attracted more than 350 participants, focusing on health, safety, and innovation in the rail industry.
articles.content_html:
National rail contractor QTS Group hosted its first safety-focused Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale, bringing together over 350 colleagues, supply chain partners, and activity hosts.

The two-day event, which took place recently, was designed to promote health, safety, and innovation within the rail industry through interactive demonstrations and hands-on activities.

Attendees had the opportunity to engage with new technology and best practices from various suppliers and specialists. Jamie Marks, HSQE Manager at QTS Group, stated that the event aimed to foster knowledge sharing and strengthen relationships across the industry.

He noted the positive feedback received and expressed enthusiasm for making next year's event even larger and more impactful.

Demonstrations included the Elios 3 drone for aerial mapping, virtual reality experiences simulating drone flights, and a confined space training simulator provided by Eurosafe.

Participants also tested their skills on an excavator simulator from Flannery Plant Hire and witnessed mock aerial rescue demonstrations conducted by IRATA-trained teams.

The event not only highlighted the importance of safety in the rail sector but also provided a platform for networking and collaboration among industry professionals.

QTS Group plans to build on this success for future events, aiming to further enhance safety practices in the rail industry.

articles.title: From air traffic control to author: Ramsbottom retiree supports dementia charity
articles.excerpt: After 36 years working in air traffic control engineering, Ramsbottom resident Ged has published his debut novel Forget Me Not, with profits going to Alzheimer’s Society and around £700 raised so far.
articles.content_html:
After a 36-year career as an engineer working in air traffic control, Ramsbottom resident Ged has found an unexpected new chapter in retirement: becoming a novelist and raising money for people affected by dementia.

His debut novel, Forget Me Not, was released on 3 October 2026. Inspired by real events, the family drama follows Vera, a 91-year-old woman living with dementia, and the relatives whose responses to her illness reveal very different intentions.

At the heart of the story are difficult questions about family loyalty, protection and vulnerability. Some of Vera’s relatives want to keep her safe, while others see an opportunity to take advantage. The novel explores the pressures that dementia can place on families, and what happens when trust is tested.

Ged said the leap from engineering to fiction surprised even him. After spending more than three decades working in air traffic control, he had not expected retirement to lead to the publication of a book.

He has also given the project a charitable purpose. Ged says every penny of profit from Forget Me Not will go to Alzheimer’s Society, and that supporters have already helped raise around £700 since the novel’s release. The total is the author’s reported figure.

To make the story accessible to people who would rather borrow than buy, he has donated copies to libraries in Ramsbottom, Bury, Prestwich and Radcliffe. He hopes the books will be available for local readers to borrow soon.

Forget Me Not is available on Amazon in paperback (£9.99) and Kindle format (£2.99), with access also offered through Kindle Unlimited, according to the author’s announcement. Readers can find it at https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B0HJP695NC.

Signed copies can be requested through https://forms.gle/RPyfy2TbDMZZKEUX7, with free hand delivery offered around Bury. Readers can also follow updates about the book at https://www.facebook.com/forgetmenotanovel.

For those whose families have been affected by dementia, Alzheimer’s Society provides information, practical support and advice at https://www.alzheimers.org.uk/.

Ged hopes the novel will both find an audience and make a meaningful contribution to a cause close to many families across Greater Manchester.

articles.title: Rochdale Sleep Out raises almost £10,000 as organisers make final appeal
articles.excerpt: Supporters spent the night outdoors at the Crown Oil Arena for Petrus Community and Rochdale AFC Community Trust, with the annual charity Sleep Out now close to its £10,000 fundraising milestone.
articles.content_html:
Supporters from across Rochdale spent Friday night outdoors in solidarity with people experiencing homelessness, helping an annual charity Sleep Out raise almost £10,000.

The event, organised by Petrus Community and Rochdale AFC Community Trust, took place on Friday 9 October at the Crown Oil Arena. Participants were joined in the fundraising effort by donors and local businesses.

Petrus said the total was now approaching the £10,000 milestone and appealed for one final push to reach it. The figure is a provisional amount reported by the organisers, rather than a confirmed final total.

The Sleep Out aimed to raise awareness of housing insecurity and homelessness while giving participants a limited insight into the practical challenges of spending a night without a comfortable bed. Organisers stressed that taking part for one night cannot replicate the uncertainty and difficulties faced by people who have no safe place to call home.

Money raised will help sustain vital support for people experiencing homelessness and disadvantage. Petrus provides accommodation, housing advice, outreach, wellbeing support and opportunities to help people rebuild stability across Rochdale, Oldham and Burnley.

The partnership between Petrus and Rochdale AFC Community Trust also supports the Changing Lives programme, which uses football, wellbeing activities and pathways into education, volunteering and employment to help people experiencing homelessness or living in supported accommodation.

Last year's Sleep Out raised £7,875.52 for the two organisations. This year's organisers have thanked everyone who slept outdoors, donated or helped make the event possible.

Petrus is encouraging Rochdale residents who wish to support the final fundraising push to donate through its official website: https://www.petrus.org.uk/.

articles.title: Who
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel, showing what the oldest printed witnesses say and what is verifiable today.
articles.summary: A short guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel, showing what the oldest printed witnesses say and what is verifiable today.
articles.body:
Walkers who know Healey Dell will recognise the narrow cleft of the Spodden called the Thrutch and the little rock alcove that has long been known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel. The “Healey Dwarf” is the best‑known supernatural figure attached to that place: in local telling a tiny, ginger‑bearded person — sometimes imagined as a stone sentinel in the river — who belongs among the fairies. But the dwarf, like other elements of the Dell’s story‑map, belongs to folklore rather than to the archive of verifiable events.

The oldest printed witness for the tale that survives in wide circulation is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire. Roby collected and published local romances and legends in the early nineteenth century (his Lancashire volumes first appeared in 1829–31), and his chapter often cited as “The Fairies’ Chapel” gathers the characters and episodes — a cavern‑like cleft, a miller, a Fairy Queen and a small figure associated with the place — that later writers repeated and reshaped. Roby’s work is a primary source for the story as it was told in his era, but it must be read as a collector’s and storyteller’s account: it records oral tradition and contemporary retelling rather than offering documentary proof of supernatural events.

Later Victorian and local writers elaborated Roby’s material. A small book published in 1882, Healey Dell, or The History (in Verse) of Fairies: Meetings of the Fairy Queen and Healey Dwarf in the Fairy Chapel, gives a fully dramatised and poetical version in which a character called Healey (often pictured with a ginger beard in these retellings) is offered a place among the fairies and imagined as a stone guardian in the river. These later accounts are useful for tracking how the dwarf’s image — costume, beard and behaviour — became fixed in local imagination, but they are literary treatments rather than independent contemporary testimonies.

On the ground today the concrete facts are straightforward and separate from the stories. Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve with visible industrial archaeology — mill remains, waterfalls and the Victorian viaduct — and a heritage centre that presents the site’s history and folklore for visitors. The rock formation that inspired the name Fairies’ Chapel is a water‑worn niche; the site was altered by extreme flooding in the 1830s, and the physical features visible now are not identical to those seen by earlier visitors. Local authorities and the heritage centre present the dwarf and related tales as part of the Dell’s living folklore rather than as documented historical personages.

What we can say with confidence: the Healey Dwarf is a figure of local tradition preserved in nineteenth‑century printed collections and in later local retellings. The earliest reliable printed appearance is John Roby’s collection; later writers — including the 1882 verse volume — shaped the dwarf’s popular image. What cannot be verified from official records is any claim that a living dwarf or a supernatural guardian actually inhabited the Dell: there are no archival documents, legal records or contemporary official investigations that establish such a thing as historical fact.

If you want to explore the sources, read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the earliest widely available printed version and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s material and Rochdale Borough Council’s site listings for the reserve’s geology, industrial remains and how the folklore is presented to visitors today. The story of the Healey Dwarf is best approached as local folklore — a useful lens on how people in and around Healey have imagined their landscape over two centuries — and as an example of the way place, geology and human storytelling become entangled.

Visiting the Dell remains the most direct way to meet the tradition: the rock alcove, the Thrutch, the viaduct and the heritage displays are all real; the dwarf lives in the stories people tell there.

A small book published in 1882, Healey Dell, or The History (in Verse) of Fairies: Meetings of the Fairy Queen and Healey Dwarf in the Fairy Chapel, gives a fully dramatised and poetical version in which a character called Healey (often pictured with a ginger beard in these retellings) is offered a place among the fairies and imagined as a stone guardian in the river. These later accounts are useful for tracking how the dwarf’s image — costume, beard and behaviour — became fixed in local imagination, but they are literary treatments rather than independent contemporary testimonies.

On the ground today the concrete facts are straightforward and separate from the stories. Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve with visible industrial archaeology — mill remains, waterfalls and the Victorian viaduct — and a heritage centre that presents the site’s history and folklore for visitors. The rock formation that inspired the name Fairies’ Chapel is a water‑worn niche; the site was altered by extreme flooding in the 1830s, and the physical features visible now are not identical to those seen by earlier visitors. Local authorities and the heritage centre present the dwarf and related tales as part of the Dell’s living folklore rather than as documented historical personages.

What we can say with confidence: the Healey Dwarf is a figure of local tradition preserved in nineteenth‑century printed collections and in later local retellings.

The earliest reliable printed appearance is John Roby’s collection; later writers — including the 1882 verse volume — shaped the dwarf’s popular image.

What cannot be verified from official records is any claim that a living dwarf or a supernatural guardian actually inhabited the Dell: there are no archival documents, legal records or contemporary official investigations that establish such a thing as historical fact.

If you want to explore the sources, read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the earliest widely available printed version and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s material and Rochdale Borough Council’s site listings for the reserve’s geology, industrial remains and how the folklore is presented to visitors today. The story of the Healey Dwarf is best approached as local folklore — a useful lens on how people in and around Healey have imagined their landscape over two centuries — and as an example of the way place, geology and human storytelling become entangled.

Visiting the Dell remains the most direct way to meet the tradition: the rock alcove, the Thrutch, the viaduct and the heritage displays are all real; the dwarf lives in the stories people tell there.

articles.title: Ten years without answers: the continuing search for Rochdale’s Jack Stewart
articles.excerpt: Jack Stewart vanished from Spotland on 8 February 2016. His missing-person appeal remains listed a decade later. Here are the original clothing details, what the community did, and how to report information safely.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Daily | Missing persons appeal | 12 October 2026

Ten years after Jack Stewart disappeared from Spotland, a national missing-person charity continues to carry his photograph and an appeal for information. Jack was last reported seen at about 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, at his home on Ings Lane in Rochdale. What happened next remains unknown in the public appeal. For anyone who remembers that morning, or who notices something potentially significant while walking in the area, information can still be passed directly to the police.

Jack's appeal is currently listed by the independent charity Missing People, with reference 16-000774. The charity records him as 68 when he went missing; some original police reporting described him as 69. The important details are the date, location and identifying information, rather than trying to resolve that inconsistency without original records.

Official Missing People appeal: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

THE MORNING JACK WAS LAST SEEN

At around 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, Jack was seen at his home on Ings Lane, Spotland. Police said his disappearance was extremely out of character, noting that he liked routine in his life. That detail matters because those familiar with his everyday movements may be able to distinguish an ordinary journey from a change in habit. The information available publicly does not establish which direction he travelled, what happened after 8am or why he disappeared.

Contemporary reports describe Jack as a white man, approximately 5ft 9in tall, with brown-and-grey hair worn in a distinctive 'teddy boy' style. His clothing was described in early coverage as a BLACK QUILTED JACKET, BLACK JEANS, STRIPED SOCKS and a DARK-COLOURED CHECK SHIRT. These are the last publicly reported clothing details, not proof that any item would remain recognisable today. Colours, fabrics and descriptions may change over time. The police are best placed to assess the significance of any discovery.

Sources: original 2016 Greater Manchester Police appeal, reproduced in subsequent MEN coverage https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/police-new-appeal-over-missing-10871344; later account with clothing description https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas; charity appeal https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

HOW ROCHDALE RESPONDED

Local people helped to look for Jack soon after he disappeared. Later reporting records that around 60 members of the public joined a search organised from Brotherod Community Centre, near his home. The response reflected a community unwilling to let a neighbour vanish without notice. Those efforts did not produce a publicly confirmed resolution in the records reviewed for this report.

Source: Manchester Evening News coverage of historic missing Greater Manchester residents https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas

JACK AS A PERSON, NOT JUST A MISSING PERSON

Jack was known to police as someone who valued routine. That is one small glimpse of the life behind the appeal: a man whose ordinary day was sufficiently familiar that his absence immediately stood out. Rochdale Daily has not been able to verify specific hobbies, employment history, or details about a wife, partner, children or surviving relatives from reliable public sources. We will not speculate about them or print supposed family memories without permission.

Anyone close to Jack who wishes to share family-approved memories of his interests, favourite places, the things that made him laugh or his daily routine may contact the newsroom. There is no expectation that relatives should speak publicly. Their privacy and wellbeing come first, and the missing-person appeal does not require the family to relive events for others' curiosity.

TEN YEARS ON: NO CONCLUSIONS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

Jack's continued listing on Missing People means the public appeal has not been withdrawn on the charity's site at the time of this report. It does not establish that he died, that he was harmed by another person, or that the police are pursuing any particular theory. The precise investigative status, searches undertaken since 2016 and any new leads have not been confirmed in a current statement from Greater Manchester Police.

A decade passing does not turn an unverified theory into fact. Whether someone remembers a sighting, has a dated photograph or recalls an unusual circumstance, even a detail that seemed insignificant at the time may be worth submitting to the officers responsible.

IF YOU ARE WALKING YOUR DOG AND FIND SOMETHING CONCERNING

If you come across clothing, personal effects, bones or other material that might be connected to a missing-person case, DO NOT try to decide yourself whether it belongs to Jack. Many items will have entirely unrelated explanations.

If you suspect you have found human remains or a scene requiring an urgent police response, call 999. Do not touch, move, uncover, collect or take anything home; do not dig or disturb the surrounding ground. Keep children and dogs away and avoid walking through the immediate area. Move to a safe position, note the location using a nearby landmark or phone map pin if it is safe to do so, and wait for police instructions.

For a non-urgent recollection, possible sighting or information about the 2016 disappearance, contact Greater Manchester Police on 101 or via https://www.gmp.police.uk. Tell the operator this concerns Jack Stewart, missing from Spotland on 8 February 2016, and provide the Missing People reference 16-000774 as an identifying aid. A charity reference is not necessarily a police incident number.

Please do not post photographs of potentially sensitive evidence, suspected remains, or unverified names online. Do not organise an unsupervised search of private land, woodland or waterways. Any possible discovery should go straight to police, who can preserve and assess evidence and contact families appropriately.

General official guidance on missing-person sightings and reporting: https://www.gov.uk/report-missing-person; UK Missing Persons Unit: https://www.nationalcrimeagency.gov.uk/missingpersons

WHAT IF YOU SIMPLY REMEMBER SOMETHING?

People who lived or worked around Ings Lane, Spotland or neighbouring areas in February 2016 might remember a morning journey, conversation or circumstance that they never associated with the disappearance. You do not need to be certain that a memory is significant before discussing it with police. Explain how confident you are, distinguish what you personally saw from what someone else told you, and do not guess to fill gaps.

The charity Missing People also accepts information confidentially. Call or text 116 000, or use the 'Report a sighting' link at https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774. Contacting the charity should not delay a call to police where there is an immediate danger or potential crime scene.

HELP FOR FAMILIES, FRIENDS AND ANYONE AFFECTED

The experience of an unresolved disappearance can affect loved ones and entire communities for years. Missing People offers free, confidential practical and emotional support to relatives, friends and people who are missing themselves. Call or text 116 000. Its family support team can also be reached at family.support@missingpeople.org.uk. Its helpline website lists current operating hours.

Missing People family help: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/help-services/family-support; helpline: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/helpline. If you are distressed by something you have encountered, the police or an appropriate health professional can advise on immediate support; Samaritans offers someone to talk to at any hour on 116 123.

ANY INFORMATION MAY MATTER

Jack Stewart was last seen in Rochdale on 8 February 2016. The clothing described in early appeals — a black quilted jacket, black jeans, striped socks and a dark check shirt — remains a potentially useful historical reference, but identification is the responsibility of trained police and forensic professionals.

For his loved ones, what matters is not speculation but a reliable answer. Ten years later, anyone with real information can still help by passing it to the right people. Rochdale Daily invites Greater Manchester Police and Jack's family, if they wish, to provide any verified updated details for a correction or follow-up; no family member is being asked to take part publicly.

Sources: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774; https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas; https://www.gov.uk/report-missing-person

articles.title: 21 years in England's bottom 100: Central Rochdale neighbourhood ranked 24th most deprived
articles.excerpt: Government figures show a part of Central Rochdale ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every index since 2004. Where did regeneration funding go — and what can actually be proved about residents' outcomes?
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

A small part of central Rochdale has been ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every national assessment since 2004. In the latest official figures it is 24th out of 33,755 areas — and one of just three places in England to have remained in that bottom 100 across all six releases over 21 years.

The finding is not an opposition-party accusation or a campaign slogan. It appears in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government's English Indices of Deprivation 2025. Its code is E01005482, its statistical name Rochdale 010C, and it falls within the wider Central Rochdale and Mandale Park area.

Official sources: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025 statistical release https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release; Government neighbourhood explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; Government research report https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-research-report

2004. 2007. 2010. 2015. 2019. 2025.

The government's researchers identified only three neighbourhoods that were among the 100 most deprived in every one of those six releases: Rochdale 010C, Middlesbrough 003F and Wirral 011C. The government's research report places the Rochdale neighbourhood within the middle-layer area known as Central Rochdale and Mandale Park.

This is not a description of the whole borough and not even of all Central Rochdale. A Lower-layer Super Output Area is a small census-based statistical area, typically home to around 1,500–1,600 people. The boundary of the LSOA matters when discussing local projects and spending. The Department for Education, for example, locates Whitehall Academy on Whitehall Street inside Rochdale 010C, confirming part of the geography, but the area cannot be equated simply with all of Mandale Park or Rochdale town centre.

Source: Department for Education establishment record for Whitehall Academy, LSOA Rochdale 010C https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/151391

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRIVING THE RANKING?

The 2025 government neighbourhood explorer states that employment deprivation is among the area's most severe problems: fewer than 1% of English neighbourhoods rank as more employment deprived. Rochdale 010C also ranks as the most deprived neighbourhood within the borough for income, with higher-than-usual income deprivation affecting children and older people.

The national index measures seven different types of deprivation: income, employment, education, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, and the living environment. Income and employment carry the largest weights at 22.5% each. In other words, the central issue here is not whether a street looks attractive after regeneration; it is the resources and opportunities available to the people who live there.

Source: Government deprivation explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; methodology and domain weights https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

DOES THIS PROVE THAT ROCHDALE HAS BECOME POORER?

No. The government explicitly warns that deprivation rankings describe RELATIVE circumstances. They do not, on their own, measure absolute changes in poverty, wages, health or household income. Boundaries and methods have changed; the 2025 index includes 55 indicators rather than 39 in 2019. Residents could have experienced improvements while their area's national relative position remained extremely poor.

But staying among the 100 most deprived on six separate occasions is nonetheless compelling evidence of persistent relative disadvantage. A serious assessment of whether interventions worked requires more than a new building or investment headline: longitudinal data on earnings, employment, child poverty, housing quality, health and skills, combined with a clear account of which projects actually reached Rochdale 010C.

Source: Government statistical release and guidance https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

THE REGENERATION MONEY: BIG HEADLINES, BUT WHICH STREETS?

In a 2023 article, Labour council leader Neil Emmott described a £400 million Rochdale town-centre investment programme, including projects such as Riverside, Upperbanks and the restored Town Hall. The council also says the town secured £23.6 million from the government's Towns Fund, intended to support regeneration, skills and connectivity over a wider geographic area. These are genuine funding and development announcements.

Yet neither £400 million nor £23.6 million is an audited total spent exclusively within Rochdale 010C. The figures include a range of projects, investment types, funding sources and locations. Treating either sum as money spent on the approximately 1,600 residents of this one neighbourhood would be misleading.

Sources: Rochdale Council leader's 2023 regeneration statement https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-leaders-blog/investing-future-boroughs-regeneration-continues; council Towns Fund overview https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/business-licensing/towns-fund-money-help-us-improve-rochdale

One more closely relevant entry does appear in Rochdale's formal capital programme: the 2025/26 budget shows £450,000 in external grant funding scheduled for 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale', described as land acquisition and remediation before homes are built by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing and private developers. An earlier programme showed £360,000 scheduled in 2023/24 for the similarly named project.

But these are BUDGET entries, not proof that either amount was actually spent. 'Central Rochdale' is also a broader project designation than LSOA Rochdale 010C. The missing link is a project-by-project ledger with actual expenditure, precise sites, housing completions and beneficiary outcomes.

Sources: Rochdale capital programme 2025/26 to 2029/30, 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale' https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s112547/Append.%201%20for%20Capital%20Programme%20202526%20to%20202930.pdf; 2023/24 capital programme https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s94502/Append.%205%20for%20Budget%20Report%20202324.pdf

WHAT HAS BEEN DONE ABOUT POVERTY?

The council approved 'The Future We Deserve', its borough-wide 2024–2029 anti-poverty strategy, in March 2024. The authority described rising destitution and inequality as reasons for taking a long-term approach. From April 2026 it also began allocating around £5 million in government-backed Crisis and Resilience Fund support across the borough to assist residents facing emergencies, housing pressures and the cost of essentials.

Those programmes matter. They are also different in purpose from capital investment: emergency food and housing support can reduce immediate hardship, while regeneration may seek longer-term jobs and productivity. Neither a borough-wide budget nor a policy document establishes how many residents of Rochdale 010C received support or whether the area's underlying deprivation indicators improved.

Sources: March 2024 Cabinet decision approving anti-poverty strategy https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=55806&Opt=3; council Crisis and Resilience Fund https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund

THE COUNCIL'S OWN RESPONSE TO SOCIAL MOBILITY CONCERNS

In a 2025 response to a social-mobility investigation, Rochdale Council acknowledged significant poverty, deprivation and inequality while pointing to improvements in town centres, education, employment opportunities and transport. It highlighted Rochdale Sixth Form College, Hopwood Hall College, the restored Town Hall and wider development proposals as assets that could improve opportunity.

These represent reasonable arguments for regeneration. But they are evidence of provision and investment, not by themselves proof that low-income residents in Rochdale 010C have entered stable, well-paid work or escaped hardship. This investigation has not obtained an LSOA-specific outcomes evaluation to test that claim.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council response to the Independent Commission on Social Mobility, 2025 https://socialmobility.independent-commission.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Rochdale-Borough-Council-response-to-Deep-dives_-a-local-perspective-on-social-mobility.docx.pdf

WHO SHOULD ANSWER?

Rochdale Council is Labour-controlled, led by Councillor Neil Emmott. The Central Rochdale ward is represented in October 2026 by Councillor Farooq Ahmed (Workers Party of Britain), Councillor Waqar Khan (Workers Party of Britain) and Councillor Sameena Zaheer (Labour and Co-operative), who also holds a Cabinet portfolio for Corporate, Governance and Transformation. The ward is a different boundary from the statistical neighbourhood and its current councillors did not all serve throughout the 21-year period.

These affiliations identify democratic responsibility and representation; the deprivation index does not establish misconduct, negligence or causation by any individual councillor or political party.

Sources: Council councillor directory https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7214; https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=5385; Workers Party councillor directory https://www.workerspartygb.org/our_councillors; council control https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/councilmeetings

SEVEN QUESTIONS THAT DESERVE DOCUMENTED ANSWERS

1. Which completed, current and planned projects since 2004 have physically overlapped the boundary of LSOA E01005482?

2. For each project, how much public funding was approved, contracted and actually spent — separated from private investment and borough-wide allocations?

3. What proportion of jobs created or safeguarded under those programmes went to residents of this exact neighbourhood, and at what wages?

4. How have child income deprivation, employment deprivation, housing conditions and school attendance changed in absolute terms over time, not merely national rankings?

5. What specific measurable targets did the 2024–2029 Anti-Poverty Strategy set for the most deprived neighbourhoods, and how does Rochdale 010C perform against them?

6. What data will the council use to demonstrate that forthcoming developments are benefiting the people already living in this neighbourhood, rather than simply changing the appearance or population mix of nearby streets?

7. Will the council publish an independently auditable, geographically itemised account of 20 years of spending and outcomes, and allow residents to examine the results?

WHY IT MATTERS

Rochdale's new shops, college provision, housing developments, town-hall restoration and cultural attractions are visible and can produce genuine benefits. The government's latest deprivation statistics show a different and equally important side of local economic life: one neighbourhood has remained among England's most deprived in every national index for more than two decades.

That is not proof that £400 million was wasted. It is proof that the success of regeneration cannot be established from the value of construction projects alone. The ultimate test is whether residents gain lasting opportunities, better homes, improved health and higher disposable incomes.

Rochdale Daily is inviting the council, its regeneration agency, the ward councillors, relevant public bodies and local community organisations to provide a full geographic spending-and-outcomes breakdown and their responses to these findings. articles.title: Rochdale Pioneers Museum hosts archive sessions on local folklore
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will hold free drop-in sessions this weekend, exploring traditional and supernatural tales from the borough's archives, led by Mitch Robinson.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will host free archive creative drop-in sessions this weekend, focusing on traditional, unusual, and even supernatural tales from the borough's archives. The sessions, led by Mitch Robinson, aim to uncover hidden stories and records, ranging from folklore to magical narratives.

Scheduled for Saturday, October 15, the hour-long sessions will take place at 12.30pm and 2pm, with no prior booking required.

Participants will have the opportunity to engage with old books, documents, and letters that often remain stored away, providing a unique insight into the area's history.

The Co-op Heritage Trust, which is facilitating the event, encourages anyone interested in storytelling, history, or creativity to attend. The sessions are particularly suitable for families with older children, as they will delve into themes of folk belief, magic, and the supernatural.

This initiative is part of the 'Open with Care!' programme, designed to inspire and engage the community during the spooky season. Attendees can expect a creative and thought-provoking experience, whether they are history enthusiasts or simply looking for an intriguing activity this weekend.
