articles.summary: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.body:
Anyone from Rochdale who’s ever limped away from a small mishap will recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” For many locals, cruckle means the particular half‑twist or awkward roll of the foot you can often walk off — not a full sprain but a sudden wobble that makes you wince. This usage is recorded in contemporary perceptual descriptions of Greater Manchester speech and has been listed by residents when describing Rochdale’s spoken character. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

The word itself, however, has deeper roots. Historical dialect lexicography gives us a family of related forms — crookle, crukle, cruggle, krukel — all clustered around meanings such as to bend, make crooked, stoop, huddle or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect sources and Scottish dialect records preserve these cognates, showing the same phonetic shape and similar senses across northern English and Scots varieties. In the Dictionary of the Scots Language you can see cognate entries (kruggle / cruggle / cruckle) used with senses like “to crouch or huddle,” and nineteenth‑century dialect glosses list crookle with senses such as “to make crooked; to bend, twist.” ([dsl.ac.uk](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd00075099))

How did a general sense of bending or crookedness come to mean the small ankle‑roll in Rochdale? Linguists point to ordinary, well‑attested word‑formation processes. A crook/crook‑ family root (suggesting bending, hooking or crookedness) plus a frequentative or diminutive ‑le ending can produce verbs that describe small, repeated, or imitative actions — crook → crookle. Comparable northern and Germanic dialect forms show similar semantic shifts from ‘bend’ or ‘stoop’ toward senses connected with awkward gait or limping; the broader comparative work on Germanic dialect vocabularies helps explain why these forms and meanings sit together. In short, cruckle is linguistically predictable as a local survival and narrowing of an older dialect verb family. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/The_semantic_development_of_words_for_%22walk%2C_run%22_in_the_Germanic_languages_%28IA_semanticdevelopm00ihririch%29.pdf))

Is cruckle uniquely Rochdalian? The short answer is: socially, yes — geographically, not absolutely. Perceptual dialect research carried out in Greater Manchester (2024) collected people’s mental maps and comments about local speech; among the keywords used to evoke Rochdale speech were “broad,” “flat,” “guinnel” and “cruckle,” showing that residents and neighbours associate the word particularly with Rochdale. That kind of folk‑linguistic visibility gives a strong local identity to a word even when related forms appear in older records elsewhere. At the same time, historical dictionaries and place‑name evidence show related spellings and senses across northern England and Scotland, so it would be misleading to claim the sound‑type has never occurred outside the area. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Large projects that collect lived speech and crowd‑sourced dialect entries also help explain how such words persist. When the British Library and other public call‑outs gathered regional words, contributors highlighted locally specific items that researchers had not always recorded in older printed dialect dictionaries; popular reportage of that work singled out “cruckle” as an example of a recognisably local term with onomatopoeic appeal. These crowdsourced attestations, together with formal perceptual surveys, are why small words like cruckle keep turning up in contemporary studies of regional identity. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? Cruckle matters because it shows how vocabulary anchors place: the word’s form and original sense are old and shared across northern dialects, but memory, everyday use and local attitude have made it feel distinctly Rochdale. Linguists view it as a useful data point — for historical contact between Lancashire and Yorkshire varieties, for small‑scale semantic narrowing, and for how people use language to say where they’re from. If you’ve got family pronunciations, old spellings or written examples from letters, keep them — local archives and dialect projects welcome material that helps trace exactly when and where words like cruckle shifted meaning and stuck to a place.

articles.title: Did Robin Hood really come to Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.summary: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.body:
There is a pulpit-shaped rock, a narrow pool and a name — the Fairy Chapel — at the base of Healey Dell’s steep gorge. The visitor centre and local heritage guides record a set of vivid stories: a King of the Fairies who turned a coven to stone, a ring lost in the river that cost a would‑be heir his title, and an origin tale that sends “Robert of Huntingdon” on the road to becoming Robin Hood. These versions are the ones you’ll see on site interpretation and in the Heritage Centre’s write‑ups. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

That is folklore, not archival evidence. The most systematic scholarly account of the Dell is an archaeological desk‑based assessment carried out for Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council by the University of Manchester Archaeological Unit in December 2004. It maps the valley’s mills, lodges, railway viaduct and later Victorian and industrial remains; it lists the local archives and printed sources consulted (John Rylands, Lancashire Record Office, Rochdale Local Studies and others) and documents the Dell’s long industrial and landscape history — but it does not produce contemporary medieval records linking a historical Robin Hood or a Robert of Huntingdon to Healey Dell. Put bluntly: the detailed desk‑based study records place, industry and later antiquarian interest, not a medieval outlaw’s itinerary. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

Healey Dell’s real, verifiable past is useful and interesting in itself. The site is a designated local nature reserve and a managed visitor attraction, with a Victorian railway viaduct that is Grade II listed and the valley’s surviving mill archaeology. Rochdale Borough Council describes the reserve, the visitor centre’s pictorial displays and the family‑oriented Fairy Grotto as part of the attraction visitors can find at Dell Road, Healey. The viaduct and the visible industrial remains are the kinds of things that the archaeological assessment and Historic England record in statutory listings. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

How did the Robin Hood story arrive here? Local legends often accrete around striking landscape features; caverns, pools and ravines attract tales of fairies, witches and enchanted tokens across Britain. The Healey Dell accounts appear in local storytelling and modern retellings by the Heritage Centre and local guides: they make no claim to derive from contemporary medieval documents but preserve a late tradition tying a Huntingdon name and a lost ring to the Chapel. Those popular accounts are part of the Dell’s cultural history and of local imaginative life — important for tourism and local identity — but they do not equal documentary proof. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

On the bigger question of Robin Hood’s historicity, mainstream scholarship treats Robin Hood as a legendary figure built from ballads and popular tales rather than a single, verifiable medieval person whose movements can be read off local court rolls. Modern reference works and folklorists stress the ballad tradition and its late medieval and post‑medieval formation; many local Robin Hood claims around England are later inventions, popular attributions or imaginative explanations for landscape oddities rather than recordable events. That does not make the stories worthless — it makes them folklore. ([books.google.com](https://books.google.com/books/about/Oxford_Dictionary_of_English_Folklore.html?hl=en&id=w2BMSAAACAAJ&output=html_text))

So what can a reader reasonably take away? If you mean “is there documentary, contemporary medieval evidence that Robin Hood or Robert of Huntingdon passed through Healey Dell?” the answer is: no such evidence has been produced in the local archival and archaeological surveys cited by the University of Manchester assessment and by the council’s heritage material. If you mean “are there stories that people tell about Robin Hood, witches and a magic ring here?” the answer is yes — they are recorded in local guides and on site interpretation, and they help make the place culturally lively. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

If you want to read more or check sources yourself: the University of Manchester archaeological desk‑based assessment (2004) is the most thorough published study of Healey Dell’s historic fabric; Rochdale Borough Council holds the reserve’s visitor information; the Healey Dell Heritage Centre publishes the Fairy Chapel story used in interpretation. None of these sources substitutes for a named medieval document placing Robin Hood in the Dell — and until such a record appears, the Robin Hood connection belongs to folklore rather than local history. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

articles.title: RBH football team takes part in Housing Association Charity Cup 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing colleagues took part in the Housing Association Charity Cup 2026 after weeks of training, with the team already looking ahead to next year's tournament.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing's football team joined eight other housing providers for the Housing Association Charity Cup 2026 at Goals Manchester.

The tournament followed weeks of preparation from RBH colleagues, who gave up their own time to train every Wednesday at the Soccer Factory in Castleton.

While Team RBH did not bring home the trophy, the organisation said the tournament was a successful opportunity for colleagues to come together and enjoy some friendly competition.

Salix Homes won the 2026 cup, while RBH congratulated everyone who took part and represented the organisation.

### Looking ahead to next year

RBH thanked Chris Hudspith, its Multi Trade Co-ordinator, for arranging the training sessions and encouraging colleagues to get involved.

Hudspith said the football programme had been a positive experience and an opportunity to meet people from other teams and departments while taking part in a shared interest.

Martin Platt, an IT Trainer, said the team came away from the tournament feeling that some close games could have gone differently, adding that they hoped to return next year and win the trophy.

RBH also said it is hoping to have a women's team competing in next year's tournament.

articles.title: Rochdale Foodbank receives more than 430kg of Harvest donations from local churches and school
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Foodbank has received more than 430kg of food donations from six local churches and a school as part of this year's Harvest Appeal.
articles.content_html: Rochdale Foodbank has received more than 430kg of food donations from local churches and a school as part of this year's Harvest Appeal. The latest donations came from six organisations across the borough, with a combined weight of 431.5kg. ### Latest Harvest donations The donations received were: - Norden Methodist Church — 46kg - St Mary's School and Church, Balderstone — 150.5kg - St Andrews Church, Entwistle Road — 57kg - St James Church, Milnrow — 63.5kg - St Mary's in the Baum, Rochdale — 78.5kg - Unitarian Church, Rochdale — 36kg Rochdale Foodbank thanked the churches, school and its volunteers for their contributions and said it has received a strong response to this year's Harvest Appeal. Representatives from the donating organisations were pictured alongside Rochdale Foodbank volunteers as the latest donations were received. The foodbank said the response demonstrates the support available from people and organisations across the local community during its Harvest Appeal. Source: Rochdale Foodbank. articles.title: Christ Church Healey to hold Harvest celebration and special bell-blessing service
articles.excerpt: Christ Church Healey will hold its Harvest service on 18 October, followed by a special afternoon service to bless the church bells with the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark.
articles.content_html:
Christ Church Healey will hold its Harvest celebration on Sunday 18 October, with the church also welcoming the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark for a special service to bless its bells later the same day.

The Harvest service begins at 10am. The church is asking those attending to bring donations of non-perishable food, which will be given to the food bank.

A second service will take place at 2pm, when the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark will join the congregation for a special service to bless the bells.

The bell-blessing service will be followed by light refreshments in the church hall.

Christ Church Healey is inviting members of the local community to join both services and take part in the day's celebrations.

articles.title: Remembrance and reflection walks offer bereaved service families a place to connect at Denehurst Park
articles.excerpt: Get Together After Serving CIC invites families, partners and loved ones to a gentle weekly remembrance walk at Denehurst Park in Rochdale, with no pressure to talk about loss.
articles.content_html:
A weekly remembrance walk in Rochdale is offering families and loved ones of fallen service personnel a chance to find companionship, fresh air and a little space to reflect.

Organised by Get Together After Serving CIC (G.A.S-CIC), the Remembrance & Reflection Walk takes place every Wednesday at Denehurst Park. Participants are invited to meet outside Denehurst Café at 12.30pm before setting off together.

The gentle walk is expected to last between 30 minutes and an hour, depending on the weather. Dogs are very welcome, although there is no need to bring one to take part.

At the heart of the initiative is the understanding that grief does not always need words. Those attending can share memories of someone they have lost, chat about everyday life, walk quietly or simply enjoy being in the company of people who understand.

The event poster captures that sentiment: “Sometimes you don’t need a meeting or a support group. Sometimes you just need to get outside, walk, talk and spend some time with people who understand.”

After the walk, the group plans to return to Denehurst Café for a warm drink, a slice of cake and more time together for anyone who wishes to stay.

The invitation is aimed at families and loved ones remembering fallen heroes, with partners and friends also welcome. There is no expectation to discuss personal experiences or bereavement, and those who would prefer a quiet walk will be just as welcome as those looking for conversation.

The weekly gathering brings remembrance into the everyday: not only formal ceremonies or anniversaries, but a simple opportunity to come together, one Wednesday at a time.

Walk details: Every Wednesday at 12.30pm. Meeting point: outside Denehurst Café, Denehurst Park, Rochdale. The walk lasts 30 minutes to one hour, weather permitting. Dogs are welcome, but are not required. Participants can return to the café afterwards for optional refreshments and company.

articles.title: New Awaab’s Law protections could cover millions more renters and vulnerable households
articles.excerpt: A government consultation will examine extending Awaab’s Law to private renters and other accommodation, with faster legal deadlines for landlords to tackle serious hazards such as damp and mould.
articles.content_html:
Millions more households could receive stronger legal protections against dangerous housing conditions under plans to extend Awaab’s Law beyond social housing.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government has launched a consultation on how the law could be introduced for private renters and whether similar protections should apply to other forms of accommodation.

Awaab’s Law currently provides legal deadlines for social landlords to investigate and address serious hazards, including dangerous damp and mould. The measures were introduced in memory of two-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in 2020 after prolonged exposure to damp and mould in his home.

The proposed extension could mean around nine million households are covered by new repair timescales, compared with around four million currently covered.

The consultation is considering protections for private rented homes as well as:

temporary accommodation for homeless people and families;

accommodation for young people leaving care; and

supported housing, including accommodation used by older, disabled and other vulnerable people.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said all renters should be able to expect a safe and decent home, regardless of tenure.

“Awaab’s Law is already helping to drive up standards in the social housing sector. We’re now moving to extend it to private landlords so that England’s 11 million private renters can enjoy the same protections,” he said.

The government says landlords are already required to act when serious hazards are identified. Around one in 10 private rented homes is estimated to contain a Category 1 hazard, the most serious level.

The Renters’ Rights Act has also introduced fines of up to £7,000 where serious dangers are found. Awaab’s Law would add legally defined timescales requiring action on the most serious conditions.

The consultation will help determine how Awaab’s Law should operate in the private rented sector, including the timescales for the new protections to come into force. It closes on 18 December 2026.

Generation Rent welcomed the move. Chief Executive Holly Williamson said too many renters live in homes that can harm their health and wait months for landlords to address problems.

Crisis also backed the proposals, highlighting the conditions faced by people living in temporary accommodation, including hostels and bed and breakfasts.

The Renters’ Reform Coalition said nobody should have to live in a home that makes them ill or puts their life at risk, while Independent Age said older renters can face serious problems including rats and mould and may be afraid to request repairs.

Independent Age said almost 96% of older renters it polled supported Awaab’s Law.

Become, the national charity for children in care and young care leavers, also welcomed the government’s consideration of stronger standards for accommodation used by young people leaving care.

The proposals form part of commitments in the Renters’ Rights Act and the National Plan to End Homelessness.

The government says the changes are intended to ensure dangerous housing conditions are dealt with quickly and that tenants can raise concerns without fear of repercussions.

Source: Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government.

articles.excerpt: Petrus is calling on Rochdale residents, businesses and community groups to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026 and help raise vital funds for local people experiencing homelessness and social exclusion.
articles.content_html:
Petrus Community is calling on people across Rochdale to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026, a fundraising and awareness event designed to highlight the realities faced by people experiencing homelessness while raising vital funds for local support services.

The Rochdale-based charity supports people experiencing homelessness, poverty and social exclusion across the borough. The Sleepout challenges participants to spend a night outdoors while learning more about homelessness and the support available locally.

Organisers are keen to stress that the event is not intended to replicate the experience of homelessness. Instead, it aims to encourage conversation, build understanding and raise money to support people accessing Petrus services.

Last year's inaugural Rochdale Sleepout brought supporters together from across the borough and raised £7,875.52 for Rochdale AFC Community Trust and Petrus.

The money raised has already helped launch Changing Lives, a partnership supporting people experiencing homelessness and those living in supported accommodation through football, wellbeing, education and employability opportunities.

According to Petrus, participants involved in the programme are rebuilding confidence, making new friendships, developing new skills and becoming more active members of their communities.

This year's event is also an opportunity for local businesses, community groups and individuals to get involved by taking part, sponsoring participants or making a donation.

Funds raised through the Sleepout will support Petrus' work across Rochdale, including homelessness prevention, housing support, wellbeing services, education and training opportunities, and practical support for some of the borough's most vulnerable residents.

Petrus is encouraging anyone interested in supporting the event to help spread the word and get involved.

articles.title: Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers take on 45-mile charity walk
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are taking on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October, to raise money for four causes close to their hearts.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are swapping the rugby pitch for the road as members of the groups prepare to take on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October.

The challenge is being organised to raise as much money as possible for four causes close to the participants' hearts: Springhill Hospice, the Motor Neurone Disease Association (MND), Rochdale Masters and Rugby League Cares.

Organisers are expecting the walk to be a major physical challenge, but say they want it to become about more than completing 45 miles. They are also appealing to local businesses and members of the community to get behind the fundraising effort.

Businesses are being encouraged to support the challenge through sponsorship, donations, supplies for the day or simply by sharing the fundraiser with customers, colleagues and their wider networks.

The organisers said: "We're not playing rugby for this one… we're putting the boots down and walking 45 miles!"

The group hopes that local support will help raise as much money as possible for the four causes while bringing businesses, sports communities and residents together around the challenge.

Anyone who can help with sponsorship, donations, supplies or promotion is encouraged to get in touch with the organisers.

Mandy from Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers said the group would be happy to provide photographs, route details and further information about the charities involved, as well as speak about the challenge.

articles.title: Oliver Coldman crowned champion golfer at Rochdale Golf Club Captain’s Final
articles.excerpt: Oliver Coldman has won Rochdale Golf Club’s 2026 Captain’s Final with a two-round total of 133, four shots ahead of runner-up Steve Royle.
articles.content_html:
Oliver Coldman has been crowned Rochdale Golf Club’s Champion Golfer for 2026 after winning the Captain’s Final during a weekend of competition at the club.

Coldman recorded rounds of 69 and 64 for a combined score of 133 to take the Captain’s Final title. Steve Royle finished runner-up after rounds of 67 and 70 gave him a total of 137.

The weekend also saw a series of other prizes decided. Raymond Clegg claimed Best Nett on Saturday, while Tom Wilson took Best Nett on Sunday.

Aaron Buckley won the Darren Ogden Memorial Trophy, awarded for nearest the pin in two on the 18th, with a distance of 2.13 metres. Steve George was named the lowest qualifier at 10 under par.

Rochdale Golf Club said the weekend had produced some brilliant golf despite the threat of rain, and congratulated all of the finalists and winners. The club also thanked the volunteers and staff involved in staging what it described as a special annual event.

A charity raffle was drawn during the weekend, with the club thanking supporters who bought tickets as well as the donors who supplied prizes. A full list of raffle prize winners is expected to be emailed to members over the coming days.

The Captain’s Final is one of the highlights of the club calendar, bringing together qualifiers for the concluding competition and recognising performances across the weekend.

articles.title: Homelessness, addiction and the cruelty of public condemnation
articles.excerpt: A disabled homeless man outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road has become the subject of photographs, insults and jokes online. The harder question is whether public humiliation solves anything at all.
articles.content_html:
There is a homeless man who regularly sits outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road in Rochdale. He uses a wheelchair, has one leg, and appears to have longstanding problems with drug dependency. In recent days, photographs purporting to show him using drugs have been circulated in a local social-media group, accompanied by descriptions including ‘junkie’, ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’, together with jokes about his disability.

Those comments deserve more scrutiny than the man they were aimed at.

It is entirely legitimate for residents to object to public drug use, theft, abusive behaviour or intimidation. It is legitimate for shop workers to expect protection at work. It is legitimate for parents to dislike exposing children to distressing scenes. But there is a clear moral distinction between criticising behaviour and publicly degrading a vulnerable person. Calling a homeless, disabled man a ‘scruff’ does not protect children. Making jokes about his missing leg does not reduce drug use. Posting photographs of him at what may be one of the lowest points of his life does not help shop staff, improve public safety or increase the likelihood that he enters treatment. It serves a different purpose: humiliation.

The ease with which some people have participated in that humiliation should trouble us.

The editor of Rochdale Daily has spoken to this man several times. In those encounters, he has not demanded money. He has generally asked for a drink, usually a chocolate milkshake. Other residents have independently described similar experiences. A Tesco worker has, by contrast, said that staff sometimes experience him as abusive. Both accounts may be true. Addiction, withdrawal, mental distress and homelessness do not produce consistent behaviour.

That does not make abuse acceptable. But neither does difficult behaviour grant the public permission to strip somebody of dignity.

During one conversation, the man said he had previously been prescribed methadone but stopped collecting it because he felt demeaned and discriminated against when attending the dispensing pharmacy. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that account. When asked whether he would consider restarting treatment if his medication could be dispensed somewhere he felt able to attend, he said yes.

That exchange should matter more than a photograph. It suggests that beneath the visible disorder is a person who can still discuss treatment, medication and the possibility of changing his circumstances. Yet this is precisely the sort of person whom public discussion can rapidly reduce to a caricature. Once the word ‘junkie’ has been applied, the individual disappears and only the label remains. That is not analysis. It is intellectual laziness.

Addiction is not a mysterious condition. It is extensively studied, medically recognised and strongly associated with homelessness, trauma, mental ill-health and social exclusion. National treatment statistics show that among people entering treatment for opiate problems in England in 2024–25, 41 per cent had no home of their own and 10 per cent were sleeping rough. Government research into rough sleeping published in 2025 found that 54 per cent of respondents reported a drug or alcohol misuse need during the preceding year.

These figures do not excuse criminal or antisocial behaviour. They do, however, make a mockery of the idea that addiction can be solved by simply telling somebody to ‘sort themselves out’. A person who is homeless must try to recover without privacy, stability, reliable sleep, secure storage, regular meals or often even basic hygiene. They may need to attend treatment, collect prescriptions, keep appointments, manage benefits, maintain identification documents and navigate housing applications while sleeping outside. To describe failure under those conditions as proof of moral inferiority is not toughness. It is ignorance.

One comment in the local discussion suggested that drug users should do these things ‘behind their own doors’. That statement is revealing precisely because the man in question does not have one.

Most people have the privilege of experiencing their worst behaviour privately. They can drink too much behind curtains, suffer mental-health crises in bedrooms, argue with family in kitchens, withdraw from medication under a duvet or make disastrous decisions without a stranger photographing them. A rough sleeper does not have a private sphere. His bedroom is public. His living room is public. His breakdowns are public. His addiction is public. And then the same society that has left him without a private space condemns him for failing to keep his problems out of sight. There is something deeply incoherent about that.

The man's disability makes the tone of some comments particularly ugly. Government research published in 2025 found that 80 per cent of people surveyed while sleeping rough reported a longstanding physical impairment, illness or disability. Yet a local discussion about a homeless man with one leg included jokes about his wheelchair. There is no serious public-interest argument for that. It is not community safety. It is not concern for children. It is not anger about shoplifting. It is mockery of disability, and adults should be capable of naming that for what it is.

The same applies to language such as ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’. Such terms do not describe conduct; they reduce a person to a social category deemed beneath respect. The implication is that once somebody becomes sufficiently poor, addicted or visibly disordered, ordinary standards of human decency no longer apply to the way we speak about them. That proposition should be rejected. A person's entitlement to dignity cannot depend upon whether they are pleasant enough, clean enough, sober enough or useful enough to satisfy strangers on Facebook.

Rochdale also needs to confront the practical context. The borough is already under intense housing pressure. Under Places for Everyone, Rochdale's housing requirement for 2025 to 2030 is 616 homes per year. Council material from 2025 recorded 7,681 applicants on the housing register, while more recent council reporting has referred to approximately 20,000 people relying upon the register and nearly 7,500 meeting statutory ‘reasonable preference’ criteria. Rochdale Council declared a housing emergency in 2023.

So the instruction often directed at people like this man is effectively the following: become sober, become stable, engage with treatment, organise your paperwork, maintain appointments, secure benefits and compete for scarce housing, all while sleeping outside and managing a major physical disability. That is not impossible. But anyone describing it as simple has probably never attempted anything remotely comparable.

There are also legal considerations when photographs and allegations are published online. Taking a photograph in a public place is not automatically unlawful, and Rochdale Daily is not suggesting otherwise. Identifiable images can, depending on context, constitute personal data, while publishing a photograph alongside a serious allegation of criminal behaviour raises separate legal questions.

The Defamation Act 2013 provides protection against statements that cause or are likely to cause serious reputational harm. Truth may be a defence, but that is different from saying that anything alleged on social media is lawful merely because the publisher believes it. If an identifiable photograph is accompanied by an assertion that a person is committing a criminal offence, the publisher should be in a position to substantiate what is being alleged. Rochdale Daily is therefore not independently stating that the man was consuming a Class A drug based solely on photographs and comments circulated online.

There is an additional point that some contributors may wish to consider before reaching for the camera. Vulnerability does not make somebody public property. The fact that a person's suffering occurs on a pavement does not create an entitlement to turn it into entertainment, gossip or a community spectacle. There may be circumstances in which photographing suspected criminal behaviour serves a legitimate evidential purpose. There is a substantial difference between preserving evidence for police and distributing an image among neighbours so that strangers can compete to produce the most contemptuous description of the person depicted. One is potentially evidence gathering. The other can become a form of public shaming.

And public shaming has a cost. If a person already believes that institutions regard him as worthless, if he already feels humiliated collecting treatment, if strangers photograph him and hundreds of neighbours discuss whether he is a ‘scruff’, then it should not surprise anyone if disengagement, isolation and further drug use follow. People sometimes ask why addicts do not seek help while simultaneously creating a social environment in which admitting addiction results in contempt. They demand recovery while reinforcing shame. They demand engagement while making the person feel despised. They demand that somebody rejoin society while making it clear that society would rather not look at them. Those positions are difficult to reconcile.

There is also a tendency to present compassion as naïveté. Those who have defended the man have been dismissed as ‘Karens’ or ‘do gooders’, as though refusing to join in public degradation demonstrates some failure to understand the realities of addiction. The opposite may be true. It requires very little sophistication to dislike someone behaving badly in public. It requires considerably more maturity to condemn the behaviour without enjoying the destruction of the person.

Compassion does not mean giving unlimited money to somebody with an addiction. It does not mean ignoring theft. It does not mean expecting retail workers to endure abuse. It does not mean pretending crack cocaine is harmless. It means retaining the ability to distinguish a human being from his worst behaviour. That distinction is central to every serious approach to rehabilitation.

If society genuinely wants people to recover from addiction, then those people must eventually be able to imagine themselves as something other than an addict. If every interaction reinforces that they are disgusting, worthless and permanently defined by their dependency, society should not be surprised when they behave as though there is little left to recover.

Rochdale Council lists homelessness support, drug and alcohol treatment and specialist services including Turning Point. Those services are important, but complex cases require coordination. A homeless person with a major physical disability and drug dependency may simultaneously require healthcare, treatment, medication management, benefits assistance, housing support and persistent outreach. That is difficult work. Writing ‘absolute scruff’ beneath a photograph is considerably easier. Perhaps that is part of its appeal. It allows people to experience the satisfaction of condemning a social problem without undertaking any of the difficult work involved in solving it.

There is a legitimate debate to be had about public drug use in Rochdale. There is a legitimate debate about homelessness, shoplifting, antisocial behaviour, policing, treatment capacity and the availability of supported accommodation. Those are serious subjects. Wheelchair jokes are not. Photographing a visibly vulnerable disabled man for the purpose of ridicule is not. Describing somebody at the lowest point of his life as though he were vermin contributes nothing whatsoever to the safety or wellbeing of Rochdale.

Residents are entitled to expect streets that are safe and usable. Tesco staff are entitled to work without abuse. Children should not have to encounter dangerous drug paraphernalia. Police should deal with offences where offences occur. But none of those propositions requires cruelty.

The question for Rochdale is not whether this man is admirable. He may not be. The question is whether a civilised community applies standards of dignity only to people whose lives are already in order. Most of the people commenting about him will eventually put their phones down and return home. They will have a bathroom, a bed, heating, a front door and somewhere to make their mistakes privately. He will still be outside. That difference should produce some humility.

If a community cannot look at a homeless, addicted, disabled man without turning his circumstances into entertainment, then there is more than one social problem on display. One is sitting on the pavement. The other is holding the camera.

articles.title: Can’t make it to church? Christ Church Healey invites community to join Sunday service online
articles.excerpt: Christ Church Healey is inviting people who cannot attend in person, are new to church or simply want to find out more to join its Sunday morning service online each week.
articles.content_html:
People across Healey and the wider Rochdale community who are unable to attend church in person are being warmly invited to join Christ Church's Sunday morning service online each week.

The church's weekly livestream is also open to people who may be new to church, curious about Christianity or who would simply feel more comfortable experiencing a service from home before deciding whether to attend in person.

Christ Church goes live at 9.55am every Sunday morning, allowing viewers to watch the service as it happens. Anyone who cannot watch at that time can catch up afterwards, with the service remaining available to view later.

The church said: “You are most welcome to join us for our weekly Sunday morning livestream from Christ Church. You can watch the service live as it happens, or at any time afterwards. We go live at 9.55am.”

For people who are housebound, unwell, caring for somebody, working on Sunday mornings or otherwise unable to be physically present, the livestream provides a way to remain connected with worship and the local church community.

It can also offer a gentle introduction for anyone who has never attended church before. There is no requirement to already be a member of the congregation — viewers can simply tune in from home and see what a Sunday morning at Christ Church is like.

The livestream runs each Sunday, with the broadcast beginning at 9.55am. Christ Church Healey welcomes both its existing congregation and newcomers joining online.

articles.title: Littleborough residents help boost flood resilience through Resilient Roch project
articles.excerpt: Residents at Olive Standring House in Littleborough have joined housing, council and Environment Agency teams to refresh planters while highlighting ongoing flood-resilience work across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Residents at Olive Standring House in Littleborough have been enjoying the summer sunshine while playing a part in efforts to improve flood resilience in the borough.

Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, Rochdale Borough Council, the Environment Agency and contractors joined residents to refresh planters as part of the ongoing Resilient Roch project.

The programme is supporting homes affected by the devastating Boxing Day floods of 2015 as well as properties considered to remain at risk of flooding today.

The work at Olive Standring House provided an opportunity for residents to get involved in improvements to their surroundings while drawing attention to the wider measures being introduced to make homes and communities more resilient to future flooding.

Further improvements are being rolled out across the borough, including flood doors, sump pumps and flood barriers. These measures are intended to reduce the impact on individual properties when extreme rainfall and rising water levels threaten homes.

Littleborough and the wider Pennine area have first-hand experience of the disruption flooding can cause. The Boxing Day floods in 2015 affected communities across the borough and remain an important reference point for current flood-prevention and resilience work.

The Resilient Roch programme brings together housing providers, the council, the Environment Agency, contractors and residents, combining physical protection measures with work intended to help communities prepare for future flood events.

The planter work at Olive Standring House is a smaller but visible part of that wider programme, giving residents an opportunity to participate directly while improvements continue elsewhere across Rochdale borough.

Further information was published by Littleborough Local at https://www.littleboroughlocal.co.uk/2026/08/residents-at-olive-standring-house-help.html.

The sponsorship followed a recent visit from representatives of MBF Cleaning, who wanted to understand how the company could best support local families and individuals in need.

Manuel and Janine from MBF Cleaning met with Ruth at Rochdale Foodbank to discuss the charity's work, share ideas and explore practical ways the business could make a difference.

The foodbank's van plays an important role in day-to-day operations, helping bring in supplies and donations before delivering food parcels to distribution points around Rochdale.

By sponsoring the vehicle, MBF Cleaning is helping the charity maintain that transport link and continue supporting people facing hardship across the borough.

Rochdale Foodbank is also encouraging other local businesses to consider becoming corporate partners. Companies interested in supporting the charity can find more information about partnership opportunities through Rochdale Foodbank's website.

The charity says it would welcome conversations with businesses interested in working together to support the local community.

articles.excerpt: Volunteers from Newhey's Gardening Gang have completed another major session in the local churchyard, cutting grass, tending shrub beds and cremation plots and clearing pathways.
articles.content_html:
A team of community volunteers has continued its work keeping a Newhey churchyard looking its best after another strong turnout for the local Gardening Gang.

Volunteers were back at work yesterday, tackling a substantial list of jobs across the churchyard and continuing the improvements made during previous sessions.

The group's 'buzzy bee strimmers' were out in force and completed the mammoth task of cutting all of the grass areas. Other volunteers weeded and cut back shrub beds and cremation plots, while a number of pathways were also cleared.

The work is part of an ongoing community effort to maintain and improve the churchyard, with local volunteers giving their own time to care for a space used by families, visitors and the wider Newhey community.

Organisers thanked everyone who took part, saying the churchyard continues to look great thanks to the efforts of the Gardening Gang.

Volunteer-led projects like this can make a significant difference to shared spaces, particularly where regular maintenance involves large areas of grass, established planting and paths which need repeated attention throughout the growing season.

The Gardening Gang is expected to announce another volunteering date, with residents being encouraged to watch for details of the next session.

Rochdale Daily would like to thank all of the volunteers giving their time to help look after Newhey's community spaces.

articles.title: Full house for National Emergency Briefing screening in Falinge
articles.excerpt: A community screening of the National Emergency Briefing attracted a full room in Falinge, with Rochdale councillors Tricia Ayrton and Shah Wazir joining residents for the event and discussion afterwards.
articles.content_html:
A community screening of the National Emergency Briefing attracted a full room in Falinge, with two Rochdale Council portfolio holders joining residents for the event and subsequent discussion.

Organisers have thanked everyone who attended the screening, saying it was encouraging to see such a strong turnout for the film and the conversation which followed.

Rochdale Borough Council portfolio holders Councillor Tricia Ayrton and Councillor Shah Wazir were among those attending.

Organisers thanked both councillors for remaining after the screening to listen to residents, take part in discussions and consider how the issues raised by the film could be discussed more widely.

They said the councillors left the event with a plan to help ensure the film and its message reach a broader audience.

The National Emergency Briefing brings together scientists, campaigners and public figures to discuss climate change and the risks they believe the UK faces, with contributors associated with the project including environmental campaigner Chris Packham.

The Falinge event gave residents an opportunity not only to watch the presentation together but to discuss its arguments and what they could mean at a local level.

Following the strong turnout, another community screening has already been arranged.

The next screening will take place on Thursday, September 4 at 6pm, giving residents who were unable to attend the latest event another opportunity to see the film and join the discussion.

Organisers thanked residents, guests and councillors for supporting the event and helping create what they described as an important community conversation.

articles.title: Every secondary school in Rochdale ranked: GCSEs, behaviour, attendance, Ofsted and what happens after Year 11
articles.excerpt: A parent's guide to the borough's 13 mainstream secondary schools - looking beyond GCSE league tables to behaviour, destinations, SEND provision, pastoral support and enrichment.
articles.content_html:
Choosing a secondary school is one of the biggest decisions a parent makes.

But deciding which school is "best" is considerably more complicated than looking at a GCSE league table.

A school could achieve excellent examination results while struggling with attendance. Another might have lower attainment but exceptional pastoral support, SEND provision and behaviour. A third might excel at getting pupils into college, apprenticeships or employment.

So Rochdale Daily has taken a broader look.

We have examined the latest publicly available information for the 13 mainstream secondary schools listed by Rochdale Borough Council, considering: Attainment 8; grade 5+ in English and mathematics; EBacc participation and performance; post-16 destinations; attendance; suspensions and behaviour; Ofsted findings; pastoral support; SEND provision; personal development; and extra-curricular opportunities.

The result is intended as a parent's guide rather than an official government league table.

There is also an important gap in the national data.

Why there is no Progress 8 score this year

Progress 8 would ordinarily be one of the most useful measures because it asks how much progress pupils make between primary school and GCSEs rather than simply how high their final grades are.

But the Department for Education cannot calculate Progress 8 for either 2024/25 or 2025/26 because pupils in those cohorts did not have the necessary Key Stage 2 assessment baseline following Covid disruption.

That means this year's Attainment 8 figures measure where pupils finished — not how far the school moved them from their starting point. That distinction matters.

Nationally, state-school pupils achieved an average Attainment 8 score of 46, while 45.4% achieved grade 5 or better in both English and mathematics. Across Rochdale, those figures were 40.6 and 35% respectively.

1. Hollingworth Academy, Milnrow — best academic performer

Hollingworth sits at the top primarily because its latest examination performance is significantly ahead of the Rochdale average. Its 2025 figures show an Attainment 8 score of 51.1, with 59.8% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths and an EBacc average point score of 4.48.

That means Hollingworth's Attainment 8 score was more than 10 points above the Rochdale average of 40.6 and also above the national state-school average of 46. The school's own 2025 figures similarly report an Attainment 8 score of around 51 and 60% achieving strong passes in English and maths.

There is, however, an interesting weakness. Only 22.2% entered the EBacc, compared with 40.5% nationally. And its published destination data for the 2023 leavers shows 84% of disadvantaged pupils continuing in education, apprenticeship or employment, compared with 94% of non-disadvantaged pupils nationally.

So although Hollingworth comfortably leads academically, parents should not interpret first place as meaning it dominates every measure.

Strengths: GCSE attainment, English and mathematics, broad academic performance. Watch: EBacc entry and destination gap among disadvantaged pupils.

2. Oulder Hill Leadership Academy — strongest all-round improvement story

Oulder Hill deserves to be near the top because the picture today is substantially different from that of its predecessor school. Its latest 2025 data gives an Attainment 8 score of 44.4, with 46.2% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths — the latter above both the Rochdale average and around the national level.

The more important finding comes from Ofsted. Following its January 2025 inspection, inspectors judged the quality of education, behaviour and attitudes, personal development, and leadership and management all Good.

That's particularly significant because the predecessor Oulder Hill Community School had previously been judged Inadequate before conversion to the Star Academies trust. Ofsted also confirmed that the school meets requirements for giving pupils access to information about technical education and apprenticeships.

Oulder Hill therefore performs particularly well in this ranking because it combines respectable attainment with strong independent inspection findings on behaviour, personal development and leadership.

Strengths: Behaviour, personal development, improving academic results, careers provision. Watch: Academic attainment remains below the national Attainment 8 average.

3. Wardle Academy — strong pastoral and academic balance

Wardle's 2025 Attainment 8 score was 44.1, above Rochdale's 40.6 average although still just below England's 46. Around 39.1% achieved grade 5+ in English and mathematics, also above the Rochdale borough figure of 35%.

But Wardle gets additional credit because the evidence isn't purely academic. The school was rated Good at its most recent Ofsted inspection, with inspectors reporting that pupils feel safe and happy and highlighting the strong relationships between pupils and staff and the school's pastoral approach.

Wardle also has specialist resourced SEND provision, something that may matter far more than league-table position for families of children with additional needs.

Strengths: Good Ofsted judgement, pastoral support, SEND provision, above-borough academic attainment. Watch: Results are solid rather than exceptional nationally.

4. St Cuthbert's RC High School — outstanding post-school destination performance

St Cuthbert's latest published results show an Attainment 8 score of 39.66, with 27.31% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 19% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.36. Those academic results place the school below Rochdale's overall averages.

But one number changes the picture considerably. The school reports 93.69% of pupils staying in education or entering employment after Key Stage 4.

That is precisely why simply ranking schools by GCSEs can mislead parents. St Cuthbert's examination figures are not among the borough's strongest, yet almost 94% of its leavers are progressing onwards.

Strengths: Post-16 destinations. Watch: GCSE attainment and strong passes in English and mathematics.

5. Cardinal Langley RC High School, Middleton — excellent destinations despite weaker 2025 attainment

Cardinal Langley's latest published government figures show an Attainment 8 score of 40.9, with 31.8% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 29.5% EBacc entry, an EBacc average point score of 3.46 — and 94% of leavers progressing to education, employment or an apprenticeship.

That 94% destination figure is excellent. The academic picture is more mixed: Attainment 8 is around the Rochdale average while English and mathematics strong passes remain below both borough and national levels.

Its position therefore reflects a strong record of getting pupils into their next destination even where the latest GCSE headline statistics are less remarkable.

Strengths: Destinations, post-16 progression. Watch: English and mathematics attainment.

6. Holy Family RC & CE College, Heywood — strong ethos and pastoral environment

Holy Family is particularly difficult to judge solely through a numerical league table because some of the most compelling evidence concerns school culture. Its most recent established Ofsted judgement is Good, while its denominational inspection rated the college Outstanding.

The school describes itself as an oversubscribed joint Roman Catholic and Church of England college and places a particularly strong emphasis on pastoral care, personal development and Christian ethos. For parents prioritising school environment alongside results, Holy Family deserves to sit toward the upper half of the table.

Strengths: Pastoral environment, ethos, inspection record. Watch: Parents should compare the latest individual GCSE subject outcomes when making an academic comparison with the schools above.

7. Dixons Middleton Academy — middle of the pack academically, Good Ofsted

Dixons Middleton recorded an Attainment 8 score of 40.3, with 33.6% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 42.9% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.57.

The EBacc entry rate is notable because it exceeds the Rochdale borough average and is around the national level. The school is rated Good by Ofsted, and its latest published destinations data indicates approximately 90% continuing into education, employment or apprenticeships.

The wider picture isn't perfect. Historical Parent View data collected around the 2024 inspection showed considerable disagreement among parents over behaviour and communication, although Parent View samples are voluntary and should never be treated like a representative opinion poll.

Strengths: EBacc participation, Good Ofsted judgement. Watch: Overall attainment and English/maths strong passes.

8. Falinge Park High School — around borough average with notable challenges

Government data for the predecessor establishment recorded an Attainment 8 score of 40.5, with 36.1% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 24.8% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.37. Those figures are remarkably close to Rochdale's overall results.

But Falinge serves a particularly challenging intake. Among disadvantaged pupils, Attainment 8 was 36.6, while 30.3% achieved strong passes in English and mathematics.

Interestingly, pupils with English as an additional language actually outperformed the school's overall cohort on several measures: EAL pupils recorded an Attainment 8 score of 42.6 compared with 40.5 overall. That is an important achievement which a simplistic league table would completely miss.

The school has since converted to academy status, meaning some current government tables show no comparable data under the new establishment record.

Strengths: Outcomes for EAL pupils. Watch: Overall attainment and disadvantaged-pupil gap.

9. Newhouse Academy, Heywood — behaviour stronger than academic outcomes

Newhouse recorded an Attainment 8 score of 38.9, with 29.7% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 30.8% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.26. That places academic performance below both Rochdale and national averages.

Its Ofsted picture is more encouraging. Although its 2023 inspection resulted in Requires Improvement overall, inspectors judged behaviour and attitudes, personal development, and leadership and management all Good. The school also underwent a monitoring visit in June 2025.

Newhouse has a substantial pastoral and attendance operation, including dedicated pastoral managers and an education welfare officer, with pupils' attendance monitored weekly. This is therefore another school where the headline GCSE statistics don't tell the full story.

Strengths: Behaviour, personal development, pastoral and attendance infrastructure. Watch: Academic attainment remains below borough averages.

10. Matthew Moss High School — academic outcomes currently below borough average

Matthew Moss recorded an Attainment 8 score of 39.3, with 34.3% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 26% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.37. These figures put the school slightly below Rochdale's overall attainment measures.

Its disadvantaged cohort recorded an Attainment 8 score of 34.7, with 27.5% obtaining grade 5+ in English and mathematics.

The gender difference is also substantial: girls achieved an Attainment 8 score of 42.3, compared with 36 for boys. That is potentially one of the more interesting findings in the borough and deserves further investigation.

Strengths: Some stronger performance among girls and EAL pupils. Watch: Overall attainment and attainment among disadvantaged pupils and boys.

11. Kingsway Park High School — results weak, enrichment exceptionally interesting

On GCSE figures alone, Kingsway Park would sit near the bottom. Latest government figures show an Attainment 8 score of 35.3, with around 18% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 18.7% EBacc entry, an EBacc average point score of 2.87 — and 91% progressing to a recognised destination.

But Kingsway Park is perhaps the clearest demonstration of why this ranking goes beyond GCSE results. The school has developed an unusually extensive enrichment programme aimed particularly at children living in poverty, with reported activities including Brazilian jiu-jitsu, football, boxing, lacrosse, windsurfing, theatre, free music tuition and instruments for pupils. The school has also operated practical support including a food bank and assistance for families experiencing hardship.

Headteacher Simon Ward has spoken openly about tackling behaviour problems and attempting to provide opportunities pupils might otherwise never experience.

That does not erase weak examination performance. But it means describing Kingsway Park simply as one of Rochdale's "worst schools" would be unfair and potentially meaningless to a parent whose priority is enrichment, belonging or pastoral support.

Strengths: Enrichment, pastoral intervention, opportunities for disadvantaged children. Watch: GCSE attainment remains substantially below borough and national levels.

12. St Anne's CE Academy, Middleton — strong personal-development offer but academic comparison remains difficult

St Anne's was judged Good across all criteria by Ofsted in 2024. The academy describes a broad programme of extra-curricular activities alongside updated science and IT facilities and a nurturing Christian environment open to pupils of all faiths and backgrounds. This gives it a stronger qualitative picture than a purely exam-based comparison might suggest.

Strengths: Ofsted, enrichment, personal development and ethos. Watch: Comparable current GCSE data should be considered alongside the qualitative strengths before parents make a decision.

Edgar Wood Academy — not fairly rankable yet

Edgar Wood deserves a separate category. It is a relatively new school and the 2025 government performance tables show no Key Stage 4 cohort available for meaningful comparison. Trying to put it 13th simply because GCSE data doesn't exist would therefore be ridiculous.

The important evidence instead comes from Ofsted. The academy was inspected again in June 2026, following an earlier monitoring visit in May 2025. Because it is still developing and only recently reached the point at which older pupils move through the school, Rochdale Daily considers it unranked rather than last. That distinction matters.

What the league table tells us

There isn't actually one "best school" for every child.

If GCSE results are your priority, Hollingworth Academy is currently the clear standout: its 51.1 Attainment 8 score and approximately 60% strong-pass rate in English and mathematics are comfortably ahead of the borough averages.

If behaviour and personal development matter, Oulder Hill, Wardle, Newhouse and St Anne's have particularly useful independent inspection evidence.

If SEND provision is critical, parents should look beyond league tables altogether. Wardle, for example, has dedicated resourced provision. SEND arrangements differ significantly between schools and between individual children's needs.

If destinations matter, St Cuthbert's and Cardinal Langley both report approximately 94% progressing into education, employment or other recognised destinations.

If extracurricular opportunity matters, Kingsway Park's enrichment offer stands out despite comparatively weak academic figures.

And what about attendance and suspensions?

These deserve particular attention. Across Rochdale as a whole, secondary-school suspension levels have been sufficiently high to warrant concern, but using borough-wide numbers to label an individual school would be unfair.

Suspensions can also be counter-intuitive. A school recording more suspensions may genuinely have worse behaviour. But it may instead have a stricter behaviour policy and suspend pupils for conduct another school manages internally. Likewise, low suspensions don't automatically prove excellent behaviour.

That is why Rochdale Daily considers suspension data alongside Ofsted's behaviour and attitudes judgement, attendance, persistent absence and other evidence rather than awarding points simply for having fewer suspensions.

Attendance has similar complications. Schools serving communities experiencing severe deprivation, unstable housing, chronic illness or high levels of additional need can face greater attendance problems that are not entirely within the school's control. It remains an important measure — but it requires context.

Rochdale remains behind nationally on attainment

The wider borough picture shouldn't be ignored. Across Rochdale, the averages are: Attainment 8, 40.6; grade 5+ English and maths, 35%; EBacc entry, 30.2%; EBacc average point score, 3.47. National state-school figures are: Attainment 8, 46; grade 5+ English and maths, 45.4%; EBacc entry, 40.5%; EBacc average point score, 4.09.

So although individual schools are doing exceptionally well, Rochdale as a borough continues to have a substantial secondary-attainment gap with England overall. That is arguably the biggest education story of all.

Rochdale Daily's overall guide

1. Hollingworth Academy — strongest academics. 2. Oulder Hill Leadership Academy — strongest recent all-round inspection picture. 3. Wardle Academy — strong academic/pastoral balance. 4. St Cuthbert's RC High School — excellent destinations. 5. Cardinal Langley RC High School — strong destinations. 6. Holy Family RC & CE College — strong ethos and pastoral environment. 7. Dixons Middleton Academy — solid all-round performer. 8. Falinge Park High School — around borough average, noteworthy EAL outcomes. 9. Newhouse Academy — improving with good behaviour and personal development findings. 10. Matthew Moss High School — below-average current attainment. 11. Kingsway Park High School — weak attainment but exceptional enrichment story. 12. St Anne's CE Academy — Good inspection and broad enrichment; insufficient comparable attainment evidence for a higher position. Unranked: Edgar Wood Academy — too new for a fair full academic comparison.

A word to parents

A league table should be the beginning of choosing a school, not the end.

A child with SEND may thrive somewhere completely different from the highest-scoring GCSE school. A child struggling emotionally may benefit more from exceptional pastoral support. An academically driven pupil may be better suited to a school with particularly strong examination outcomes and curriculum breadth. A child who needs confidence may flourish because of sport, music, drama or enrichment.

Parents should therefore look at results, behaviour, attendance, pastoral care, SEND provision, destinations, enrichment — and how their own child feels inside the school. That gives a much more meaningful picture than a GCSE percentage alone.

Sources and methodology: Rochdale Daily's analysis uses the Department for Education's 2025 school performance tables, latest available Ofsted inspections and monitoring visits, Rochdale Borough Council's official secondary-school list, schools' statutory published information and publicly available destination, SEND, pastoral and enrichment information. Where directly comparable current information was unavailable, this is stated rather than estimated. Progress 8 has deliberately not been used for 2025 because the Department for Education says it cannot be calculated for the current cohorts due to the absence of Key Stage 2 baseline assessments following Covid disruption.

articles.title: Got a Uniform For All order waiting? Balderstone Library needs the shelf space
articles.excerpt: The school uniform reuse scheme says its collection point is 'busier than Amazon's warehouse' - and is asking families with ready-to-collect orders to pick them up to make room for new deliveries.
articles.content_html:
Families with a school uniform order waiting at Balderstone Library are being asked to collect it as soon as possible - because the shelves are full and new deliveries are arriving fast.

Uniform For All, the borough scheme that gives pre-loved school uniform a second life, says anyone who has received an order-ready-to-pick-up email from www.uniformforall.co.uk should call in and collect it promptly to make space. "It's busier than Amazon's warehouse at the Uniform For All office right now," the scheme said.

What is Uniform For All?

Uniform For All collects donated school uniform - the coats, jumpers, polo shirts, trousers and PE kit that children outgrow long before they wear out - checks and sorts it, and passes it on to families across the borough. Orders are placed through the website and collected locally, with Balderstone Library serving as a collection and donation point.

The idea is simple but the impact is real. Kitting a child out for September can cost families well over a hundred pounds per child, and for households already stretched by rent, bills and food, uniform costs land at exactly the wrong time of year. A reuse scheme means good clothing goes to a child who needs it instead of landfill, families keep money in their pockets, and children start term dressed the same as everyone else.

With the summer holidays in full swing and the new school year only weeks away, demand is at its annual peak - hence the plea for prompt collections.

How to donate

If you have school uniform your children have outgrown, you can drop it off at Balderstone Library too. Clean, wearable items are what the scheme needs most. And if your child needs uniform for September, orders can be placed at www.uniformforall.co.uk.

articles.title: RBH warns tenants over cold-calling 'claims farmers' offering compensation for repairs
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says customers are being cold-called by firms offering 'no win, no fee' solicitors for repair claims - a warning that lands against the backdrop of the Awaab Ishak tragedy and the reforms that followed.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing has warned tenants to be on their guard after a number of customers reported being cold-called by a firm asking about property repairs.

The landlord says the callers offered to provide a solicitor to work on tenants' behalf so they could claim compensation. Firms operating this way - sometimes called claims management companies or "claims farmers" - typically describe themselves as offering "no win, no fee" services.

"Be careful - if something sounds too good to be true, it probably is," RBH said, urging anyone with a concern about their home to talk to the landlord directly so it can be sorted. Repairs can be reported via the MyRBH portal at www.myrbh.org.uk, by calling Freephone 0800 027 7769, or by emailing rbh.repairs@rbh.org.uk. RBH says it aims to get things right first time, and tenants who feel it has fallen short can find details of how to complain at www.rbh.org.uk/feedback.

Why this matters in Rochdale

No warning about housing disrepair in this borough can be read in isolation from what happened to Awaab Ishak.

Awaab was two years old when he died in December 2020. In November 2022, a coroner concluded that his death was caused by prolonged exposure to mould in his family's RBH flat on the Freehold estate - mould his parents had repeatedly reported. The case caused national outrage, cost RBH its chief executive, and led directly to Awaab's Law, which sets legal time limits for social landlords in England to investigate and fix damp, mould and other hazards, with the first phase of those duties coming into force in October 2025.

That history cuts two ways. It explains why RBH is now at pains to encourage tenants to report repairs directly and to demonstrate that reports will be acted on - rebuilding confidence that was badly damaged. And it also explains why claims firms see RBH tenants as a market worth cold-calling: disrepair claims against social landlords have grown sharply across the country, and a landlord with RBH's recent history is an obvious target for firms seeking clients.

Tenants are entitled to seek independent legal advice about genuine disrepair, and nothing prevents them doing so. But consumer bodies have long warned that some claims firms take large cuts of any compensation, sign tenants up to agreements with exit fees, or pursue claims that leave tenants worse off than simply having the repair done. A tenant's first and simplest route remains reporting the problem to the landlord - and, if it is not fixed, escalating through the complaints process and then to the Housing Ombudsman, which is free.

The test for RBH is the one Awaab's case set: whether reports of damp, mould and disrepair are fixed properly and fast, first time. If they are, the cold-callers will find little to farm.

articles.title: Shoppers donate 368 kilos of food at Rochdale Foodbank's Morrisons Kingsway drive
articles.excerpt: Generous shoppers added extra items to their trolleys over two days at Morrisons Kingsway, donating 368kg of food. How the foodbank works, how to get help - and how to give it.
articles.content_html:
Shoppers at Morrisons Kingsway have donated a remarkable 368 kilos of food to Rochdale Foodbank after a two-day food drive at the store last Thursday and Friday.

The foodbank thanked all the generous shoppers who added extra items to their shopping, saying donations came in all shapes and sizes and included many of its most needed items. The charity also paid special tribute to the volunteers who staffed the collection and made the event a success, adding that every single item received will make a big difference to its clients.

Rochdale Foodbank has been part of life in the town for more than a decade. Registered as a charity in its own right in 2017, it operates as part of the Trussell network of food banks and is run almost entirely by volunteers - around 70 of them - who sort, date-check and pack donated food into emergency parcels at its base off Newgate in the town centre.

How the foodbank works

The foodbank operates on a referral system. Care professionals - including GPs, health visitors, social workers, Citizens Advice staff, welfare officers, the police and probation services - identify people in crisis and issue them with a foodbank voucher. That voucher can then be exchanged at a foodbank session for an emergency parcel containing at least three days of nutritionally balanced food. Volunteers meet clients over a cup of tea and can signpost them to agencies able to help with the longer-term problem, from debt advice to benefits support.

Alongside its main sessions, the foodbank has expanded in recent years. A Saturday morning session runs at Branches Christian Fellowship in Smallbridge, where clients can collect parcels between 10am and 12pm, and the charity has also opened Rochdale Central Pantry in the Rochdale Exchange Shopping Centre - a membership pantry for people who have recently needed foodbank support and could use a little extra help each week.

If you need help, you can call the foodbank on 0300 102 1646 or visit rochdale.foodbank.org.uk, which lists the organisations able to issue vouchers.

How to donate

More than nine in ten items given out by Trussell network food banks are donated by the public, which is why collections like the Morrisons drive matter so much. There are permanent donation points in Rochdale's larger supermarkets, including Tesco, Asda and Morrisons, intended for food purchased in-store. Larger donations can be dropped off at the foodbank's warehouse via the Newgate service area - ring ahead on 0300 102 1646 for big deliveries - and the foodbank publishes a shopping list of the items it most urgently needs on its website. Money donations, which help cover running costs and fill gaps in donated stock, can also be made through the website.

As the foodbank itself puts it: even if it's just one tin every week, every tin helps.

articles.title: Lord-Lieutenant's visit, a surprise inspection passed and a packed cafe: quite a week for Whitworth's Stronger Together
articles.excerpt: The Whitworth carers' group welcomed the King's representative in Lancashire, retained its 5-star hygiene rating in a surprise inspection, and saw its Community Cafe overflow into the main hall — all in one week.
articles.content_html:
A remarkable week for Whitworth carers' group Stronger Together began with a royal representative at the door and ended with a cafe so busy it spilled into the main hall.

On Monday the group welcomed the Lord-Lieutenant of Lancashire, Amanda Parker, and her husband Robert. Mrs Parker is His Majesty The King's personal representative in Lancashire and the first woman to hold the role in the county in almost five hundred years, and her visit is a mark of how far the volunteer-run group has come.

The same day brought a test of a different kind: an unannounced visit from environmental health officers just before lunch service. The inspectors found everything in order and the group retained its food hygiene rating of 5, the top score, which it has held since Rossendale Borough Council first awarded it in December 2024.

By Tuesday the group's Community Cafe was packed, with every table full and half of the main hall pressed into service to seat everyone.

Stronger Together was founded in 2023 by Angela Forster and Kathleen Proctor, both unpaid carers themselves, after they found there was nowhere locally for carers to turn for support. What began as a weekly coffee morning has grown into something much bigger, now based at The Ashcroft on Market Street, where volunteers serve more than 70 fresh, home-cooked meals every week alongside cakes and unlimited drinks, all free of charge with donation pots for those who wish to give.

The group describes itself as a warm, safe space offering advice and emotional and practical support, with activities including prize bingo, crafts and quizzes, and it runs entirely on fundraising, raffles, donations and grants. A crowdfunded project launched last year added gentle exercise sessions with a qualified trainer, healthy eating advice and a singing group open to all ages and abilities.

Recognition has followed. The founders received a Mayor's Special Award at the Whitworth Business and Community Awards in 2023, with the then Mayor of Whitworth describing the pair as truly inspirational to the community. The group went on to win the Not-for-Profit category at the Rossendale Business Awards, and this summer it was shortlisted for Community Group of the Year at the Pride of Rossendale Awards.

Reflecting on the week, the founders thanked the group's volunteers and supporters, saying the group is truly blessed in the people around it.

Anyone who would like to support Stronger Together, volunteer or find out about its sessions can contact the group through its Facebook page.
